practice.stem:
Read Text 1 and Text 2, then answer the question.

Text 1: Post on the school noticeboard by a parent
The tuck shop sells crisps, fizzy drinks and sweets every single day. My son comes home with no appetite and a headache. The school teaches us about healthy eating in science lessons, so why does it sell junk food at break? If the shop sold only fruit, sandwiches, yoghurt and water, children would concentrate better in the afternoon. Other schools in Lahore have done this successfully.

Text 2: Reply posted by a Grade 10 student
I agree we should eat better, but banning everything will not work. Students will simply buy snacks from the vendor outside the gate, where nobody checks how clean the food is. Healthy items also cost more, and not every family can afford them. The tuck shop uses its profits to pay for sports equipment, so if sales fall, the cricket team suffers. A fairer idea is to offer healthy choices alongside a few treats.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your principal is deciding whether the school tuck shop should sell only healthy food. You decide to write a letter to the principal giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether the tuck shop should sell only healthy food.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Principal,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: tuck shop sells unhealthy food daily – convincing, but based on one child's experience.
Text 1: school is inconsistent (teaches healthy eating, sells junk) – strong point.
Text 1: healthy food improves afternoon concentration – plausible but no evidence given.
Text 1: other Lahore schools succeeded – vague, no names or results.
Text 2: students will buy from the gate vendor – realistic and raises a hygiene risk.
Text 2: healthy food costs more – fair, though some items (fruit, water) are cheap.
Text 2: profits fund sports – relevant but suggests money matters more than health.
Text 2: compromise of mixed choices – balanced.

Content a strong answer could use:
• School's message is inconsistent if it teaches nutrition but sells junk food
• Concentration and health benefits are likely but the parent offers only one example
• Risk that a ban sends students to the unchecked vendor at the gate – could worsen hygiene
• Cost of healthy food – could be managed by pricing fruit and water cheaply
• Loss of profits for sports equipment – could be replaced by selling healthy snacks well
• Own view, e.g. phase in mostly healthy menu with occasional treats, ask students to taste-test new items
Short model opening: I am writing as a Grade 10 student who buys lunch from the tuck shop most days, because I believe the proposal to sell only healthy food deserves careful thought before a decision is made.

Text 1: Message from a teacher in the school newsletter
From next year, every student in Grades 9 and 10 could complete forty hours of community service, such as teaching younger children to read, helping at the hospital reception or cleaning the neighbourhood. Students learn responsibility and kindness that no textbook can teach. Universities and employers also like to see this kind of experience. Last year a small group of volunteers from Grade 10 ran a reading club for a nearby primary school, and the children's teachers said their confidence grew enormously.

Text 2: Reply from a student on the school's online forum
Forty hours is a lot when we already have tuition after school and exams to prepare for. If something is compulsory, people do it half-heartedly just to get the hours signed. Some students live far away and have no transport to these places. Service should come from the heart, not from a rule. Why not reward volunteers with certificates instead of forcing everyone?

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The school is considering making community service compulsory for Grades 9 and 10. Write a letter to the principal giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether community service should be compulsory.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Principal,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: develops responsibility and kindness – likely, but not guaranteed.
Text 1: useful examples of service – shows the idea is practical.
Text 1: universities and employers value it – a fair but selfish reason.
Text 2: forty hours on top of tuition and exams – realistic workload concern.
Text 2: compulsory service done half-heartedly – plausible.
Text 2: transport problems – practical and fair.
Text 2: rewards instead of rules – positive alternative.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Value of real-life experience and empathy
• Benefit for university applications – useful but should not be the main reason
• Workload and exam pressure – could reduce hours or spread over two years
• Forced service may lose meaning; choice of activity could keep motivation
• Transport – the school could organise service on its own campus or nearby
• Own view, e.g. a smaller compulsory number of hours with free choice of activity and recognition for extra
Short model opening: I am writing to share my views on the proposal that every student in Grades 9 and 10 should complete forty hours of community service.

Text 1: Suggestion from the Year 9 class representative
For our annual trip we should visit the national museum in the capital. We will see objects from the Indus Valley civilisation that we study in history, and the museum offers a free guided tour for schools. It is also safe and indoors, which matters in the heat of May. The museum has recently opened a new gallery on the Gandhara period, with statues and coins that most of us have only seen in photographs. A day trip by train would also be easy to organise.

Text 2: Suggestion from a student in the outdoor club
A two-day adventure camp in the hills would be far more exciting. We would learn rock climbing, map reading and how to work as a team. Students spend all year in classrooms – a trip should be different. The camp costs more, but it provides all meals and trained instructors. Last year's Year 9 group went to a similar camp and still talk about it. The site also has a doctor on call and proper first-aid facilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your school is choosing between a museum visit and an adventure camp for the annual Year 9 trip. Write a letter to your principal giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about which trip the school should choose.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Principal,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: links to history syllabus – strong educational reason.
Text 1: free guided tour – keeps costs down.
Text 1: safe and indoors in May heat – sensible.
Text 2: new skills and teamwork – valuable.
Text 2: a change from classrooms – appealing but subjective.
Text 2: costs more but includes meals and instructors – honest, but some families may not afford it.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Educational link of the museum to the syllabus
• Low cost and safety of the museum trip
• Practical skills and teamwork from the camp
• Higher cost could exclude some students; safety depends on instructors
• Own view, e.g. choose one with reasons, or museum now and camp in cooler autumn
Short model opening: I am writing on behalf of many students in Year 9 who are excited about this year's trip and would like to share our views on the two choices.

Text 1: Proposal from the school IT coordinator
Our Grade 9 classes carry heavy bags of textbooks that weigh almost as much as the students. Tablets would hold every book in one place, could be updated free of charge each year, and let students search for a word instantly. Two schools in the district ran a pilot, and their test scores rose in the second term.

Text 2: Comment from a parent
I doubt a tablet can replace a real book. Children will be tempted to play games instead of reading, and a screen gives me headaches after an hour. Not every family can afford to replace a broken device, and the school has no plan for charging tablets during power cuts. Books still work when the electricity fails.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your principal is deciding whether the school should replace printed textbooks with tablets. You decide to write a letter to the principal giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether the school should replace printed textbooks with tablets.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Principal,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Content points a strong answer could use:
• Text 1: heavy bags are a real practical problem, and updates are free; the search function is a clear benefit
• Text 1: the pilot scores are a strong claim but the writer gives no detail or subjects, so the evidence is weak
• Text 2: games and distraction are a fair concern, but depend on how the tablets are controlled
• Text 2: eye strain and cost of replacing devices are practical points; the lack of a charging plan is a real weakness
• Text 2: books work in power cuts, a strength of print that Text 1 does not address
• Own view e.g. keep core textbooks, add tablets for named subjects with a budget and a charging plan
Model opening: Dear Principal, I have read the views in both texts about our textbooks. The idea of tablets is attractive, because our bags are heavy and the search tool is useful, but the evidence for better results is thin...

Text 1: Message from a Grade 11 student
Our college library closes at four o'clock, which is when most of us finish classes. Extending opening to ten at night would let students revise after dinner, and it would stop the reading rooms being empty all evening. Two volunteers could easily supervise the late shift.

Text 2: Note from the library staff
Staying open later means paying extra staff and electricity, and the budget is already tight. Students who come late often spend the evening on their phones rather than studying, and the building is quiet only if someone checks the rooms. Opening until seven and on Sunday mornings would cost much less and reach most students.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your college principal is considering whether the library should stay open until ten at night. You decide to write a letter to the principal giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether the library should open until ten at night.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.

Write 250 to 350 words.

• Text 2: extra cost and staffing are realistic concerns that the student does not answer
• Text 2: phone use in the evening is a fair point but not proven for all students
• Text 2: a shorter, cheaper alternative (seven o'clock and Sunday mornings) is a practical compromise
• Own view e.g. a trial of extended hours on two evenings a week, with volunteers trained and results reviewed

Text 1: Notice from the city development office
The city plans to convert the eastern half of Gulshan Park into a multi-storey car park. Traffic around the market is now so heavy that ambulances are delayed and shoppers circle for half an hour looking for space. The car park will hold 600 vehicles and bring in parking fees that will pay for repairs to the remaining half of the park. Construction will take eighteen months.

Text 2: Comment from a local resident on a community website
Gulshan Park is the only green space for thousands of families in flats. Old people walk there every morning and children play cricket there after school. Once trees are cut down they take decades to grow back. More parking will only encourage more cars – the traffic will return within a year. Why not run a shuttle bus from the outskirts instead? Nobody asked residents before this plan was drawn up.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write a letter to the editor of your local newspaper giving your views on the plan to build a car park in half of Gulshan Park.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether half of the park should become a car park.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Editor,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: traffic delays ambulances – serious and persuasive.
Text 1: shoppers waste time looking for parking – true but less important than health.
Text 1: fees will repair the rest of the park – attractive but a promise, not a guarantee.
Text 1: 18 months of construction – disruption the office does not discuss.
Text 2: only green space for families in flats – strong, affects many people.
Text 2: trees take decades to regrow – permanent loss, convincing.
Text 2: more parking attracts more cars – a known effect, reasonable.
Text 2: shuttle bus alternative – constructive but cost not discussed.
Text 2: residents not consulted – fair criticism of process.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Ambulance delays are a genuine safety issue that must be solved somehow
• Shopper convenience is a weaker reason than losing public green space
• Promised repair money is uncertain; the park would shrink by half
• Long construction would close more of the park for a year and a half
• Green space is vital for health of residents in flats; trees cannot be replaced quickly
• Extra parking may attract extra traffic, so the problem may return
• Alternatives: shuttle buses, an emergency-vehicle lane, parking on unused land elsewhere
• Own view with a call for public consultation
Short model opening: Sir, the plan to pour concrete over half of Gulshan Park may ease the traffic outside the market for a few months, but I fear our city would pay for it for decades.

Text 1: Proposal from the school sports department
Our large cricket ground is used for only three months a year. We propose turning half of it into courts for basketball, badminton and volleyball. These sports can be played all year, in less space, by more students at once, including girls who rarely get time on the cricket field. Courts are also cheaper to look after than grass, which needs daily watering.

Text 2: Letter from the captain of the school cricket team
Cricket is part of our school's identity – our team has won the district cup four times. A smaller ground would mean we could no longer host matches, and young players would lose the chance to be noticed by regional coaches. Many students come to this school because of its cricket. Courts can be built on the unused land behind the science block instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write a letter to the head of the sports department giving your views on the proposal to replace half of the cricket ground with courts.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about the future of the cricket ground.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Head of Sports,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: ground used only three months – strong if accurate.
Text 1: more students, all year round – persuasive about fairness.
Text 1: girls get little field time – important equality point.
Text 1: cheaper upkeep, less water – sensible, especially in a dry climate.
Text 2: cricket is school identity, cup wins – emotional, matters to some.
Text 2: no home matches, fewer chances with coaches – real cost to talented players.
Text 2: students choose the school for cricket – claim without evidence.
Text 2: alternative site behind science block – could satisfy both sides if suitable.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Fairness: more students and more girls could play under the proposal
• Efficient use of space and lower water and maintenance costs
• Loss of tradition and of opportunities for talented cricketers
• Claims about admissions and usage need checking (survey of how often the ground is used)
• Alternative site could be a compromise; cost of preparing it must be considered
• Own view with a recommendation
Short model opening: I am writing to give my views on the proposal to convert half of our cricket ground into courts, a plan that affects almost every student who plays sport at this school.

Text 1: Announcement from the town committee
From next month, street vendors will no longer be allowed on the pavements of Saddar Bazaar. Their carts block the way, forcing pedestrians onto a busy road, and food stalls leave waste in the drains. Vendors may apply for a place in the new covered market two kilometres away, where water and electricity are provided.

Text 2: Comment from a fruit seller
I have sold fruit on this corner for nineteen years. My customers are people walking home from work; nobody will travel two kilometres for a kilo of bananas. The new market charges rent that many of us cannot pay. We are willing to keep the pavement clear by using marked spaces and cleaning up each evening. Removing us will also make the street emptier and less safe at night. Many of my customers are office workers who stop for five minutes on their way to the bus stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write a letter to the chairperson of the town committee giving your views on the decision to remove street vendors from Saddar Bazaar.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether street vendors should be moved away from the bazaar.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.

Write 250 to 350 words.

Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: carts block pavements, pedestrians pushed onto road – genuine safety problem.
Text 1: waste in drains – a real hygiene issue.
Text 1: covered market with water and power – a fair offer on paper.
Text 2: 19 years, loyal passing customers – shows vendors depend on location.
Text 2: rent unaffordable – strong practical objection.
Text 2: marked spaces and cleaning – sensible compromise.
Text 2: vendors make streets safer at night – plausible, 'eyes on the street'.

• Pedestrian safety must be protected
• Hygiene and waste problems need a solution
• Vendors' livelihoods depend on passing trade; moving them may ruin them
• Rent at the new market may be unaffordable
• Compromise: licensed marked spaces, cleaning rules, fines for breaking them
• Vendors bring life and safety to the street
• Own view with a recommendation

Read Text 1 and Text 2, then answer the question.

Text 1: Report summary from the education board
We are considering adding one hour to the end of every school day for supervised homework. Teachers would be on hand to help, and students would go home with their work finished, leaving evenings free for family. Students without a quiet place to study at home would benefit most. A pilot scheme in twelve schools last year showed that students who used the homework hour handed in more of their work on time.

Text 2: Letter from a parent in a national newspaper
My children already leave home at 7 a.m. and return at 2:30 p.m. tired and hungry. Another hour would leave no time for sport, chores or simply resting. Teachers are already overworked, so who will supervise? Homework is meant to build independent study habits – doing it at school with help defeats the purpose. Children also need time to help at home, visit grandparents and play outside – that is part of growing up too.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The education board is considering adding a supervised homework hour to the school day. Write a letter to the education board giving your views.
In your letter you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether the school day should include a supervised homework hour.
Base your letter on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your letter: 'Dear Members of the Education Board,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: teacher help available – useful for weaker students.
Text 1: free evenings for family – attractive.
Text 1: helps students with no quiet place at home – strongest fairness argument.
Text 2: long day already, tiredness – realistic.
Text 2: no time for sport or rest – health concern.
Text 2: teachers overworked – fair, the board doesn't explain staffing.
Text 2: homework should build independence – thoughtful, but help is not the same as doing it for them.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Equal opportunity for students with no study space at home
• Help from teachers can stop students getting stuck
• Longer day may cause tiredness and loss of exercise
• Staffing and teacher workload need to be addressed
• Independent study habits matter, but supervision can still encourage independence

Text 1: 20,000 titles and 24-hour access – attractive and convincing.
Text 1: e-books don't go missing – true, but tablets can break or be stolen.
Text 2: libraries give a screen-free space – thoughtful point.
Text 2: memory better with print – 'research suggests' is vague but plausible.

Text 1: Article in a science magazine
Space exploration has given us weather satellites, GPS and better medical imaging. Studying other planets helps us understand climate change on our own. Exploration inspires young people to become scientists and engineers. The money spent is small compared with what governments spend on many other things. Satellites now warn farmers of droughts and help rescue teams find people after floods. Without earlier space missions, none of this would exist.

Text 2: Blog post by a development worker
Millions of people still lack clean water, electricity and schools. Every rocket launch costs enough to build hundreds of wells. Satellites are useful, but we already have them. We should solve the problems on Earth before we spend fortunes looking for life on Mars. Children in some villages still walk for hours each day to collect water instead of going to school. Their problems cannot wait for the results of a mission to another planet.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your school science club is holding a discussion on whether countries should spend money on space exploration. You have been asked to give a speech to the club.
In your speech you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether countries should spend money on space exploration.
Base your speech on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your speech: 'Good afternoon, fellow members of the science club.'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: satellites, GPS, medical imaging – real practical spin-offs.
Text 1: helps understand climate change – true, e.g. studying Venus and Mars atmospheres.
Text 1: inspiration – likely, hard to measure.
Text 1: spending is relatively small – fair, but no figures given.
Text 2: clean water, electricity, schools lacking – morally powerful.
Text 2: rocket launch = hundreds of wells – emotive comparison, no figures.
Text 2: we already have satellites – overlooks that they need replacing and improving.
Text 2: 'solve Earth first' – assumes it is either/or.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Practical spin-offs of space technology
• Satellites monitor floods, crops and weather, which helps poor countries too
• Inspiration for science careers
• Urgent human needs and moral priorities
• False either/or: budgets can do both; space spending is a small share
• Neither text gives precise figures – both rely partly on emotion
• Own view, e.g. focused, useful space programmes that support life on Earth
Short model opening: Good afternoon, fellow members of the science club. Every time you check the weather on your phone or find your way with a map app, you are using the results of space exploration.

practice.stem:
Read Text 1 and Text 2, then answer the question.

Text 1: Email from the head of IT to all staff
AI chatbots are here to stay. Instead of pretending they do not exist, we should teach students to use them well: to explain hard ideas, check grammar and generate practice questions. Students who learn this now will have an advantage at university and at work. Banning chatbots will not stop students using them at home; it will only stop teachers from showing them how to use them responsibly.

Text 2: Opinion from an English teacher
If a machine writes the essay, the student learns nothing. Chatbots sometimes invent facts with complete confidence, and students may not notice. Homework is practice, like training for a match – you cannot ask someone else to run for you. Homework should be done without them. I have already received essays that were clearly not written by the student – the style changed completely halfway through. Marking these wastes time and tells me nothing about what the student can do.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your school is deciding whether students may use AI chatbots for homework. You have been asked to give a speech to students in Grades 9 and 10.
In your speech you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether students should be allowed to use AI chatbots for homework.
Base your speech on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your speech: 'Good morning, everyone.'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: chatbots here to stay – realistic.
Text 1: useful for explanations, grammar, practice questions – genuine uses.
Text 1: advantage later – plausible.
Text 2: machine-written essays mean no learning – strong.
Text 2: chatbots can invent facts – true and important.
Text 2: training analogy – effective comparison.
Text 2: total ban – hard to enforce outside school.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Chatbots will be part of future study and work
• Helpful uses: explanation, feedback, practice
• Copying answers prevents learning
• Accuracy problems: students must check facts
• A ban is difficult to enforce at home
• Both writers agree learning is the goal – they differ on method
• Own view, e.g. allowed for explanation and checking with honesty rules; essays written by the student
Short model opening: Good morning, everyone. Some of you may already have asked a computer to help with last night's homework – so the question is not whether we will use these tools, but how.

Text 1: Statement from the roads department
Traffic on Canal Road is so heavy that buses take forty minutes to cross the town. Widening the road to four lanes would halve journey times and let ambulances reach the hospital faster. New trees planted along the verges would replace the old ones.

Text 2: Speech notes by a local conservation group
The old neem and tamarind trees on Canal Road shade the pavements, cool the air and provide homes for birds. Trees take decades to grow, and new saplings will not give the same shade for years. Widening the road will bring more cars, so the traffic problem may soon return.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The town council will meet next week to decide whether Canal Road should be widened. You have been asked to give a speech at the meeting giving your views.
In your speech you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether Canal Road should be widened.
Base your speech on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your speech: 'Honourable members,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Content points a strong answer could use:
• Text 1: a faster route for buses and ambulances is a strong, practical benefit
• Text 1: replacing old trees with new saplings does not replace the shade for many years, a flaw in the roads department's plan
• Text 2: the cooling and habitat benefits of old trees are real environmental costs
• Text 2: the argument that new traffic will refill the road is convincing but not proven with evidence
• Text 2: the text is written by a group with a clear interest in conservation, so the case should be weighed carefully
• Own view e.g. widen only the busiest junctions, protect the oldest trees and add a bus lane
Model opening: Honourable members, I rise to speak about Canal Road. Every resident feels the pain of the traffic, yet we must not...
parts.working: 25 marks: 10 for content, 15 for quality of writing. Content (10): up to 5 for evaluating ideas from both texts (saying which are convincing and why, e.g. weak evidence, one person's experience, a practical flaw); up to 5 for a clear own view with developed reasons that draw on the texts. Writing (15): 13-15 = register and format suited to the task, fluent and well-linked paragraphs, varied accurate sentences, ideas in own words; 9-12 = clear and organised, some variety, occasional lifting from the texts or errors; 5-8 = limited control of register or structure, frequent errors; 0-4 = very little relevant or accurate writing. Text 1: Message from your cousin Ayesha
I've been offered a place at a university in Malaysia to study engineering! It's exciting – I'd improve my English, meet people from everywhere and maybe get a better job. But I'd be so far away from all of you, and the fees and living costs are high. They also have a scholarship that covers part of the fees if I keep my grades high. My best friend is going there too.

Text 2: Advice from Ayesha's father
Our local universities have good engineering departments, and Ayesha could live at home and save money. She is only eighteen. Later, for a master's degree, she could go abroad when she is more mature and knows exactly what she wants. Living abroad means paying rent, food and travel, and we would worry about her every day. Family support matters when studies become difficult.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your cousin Ayesha has asked for your advice on whether she should study abroad or at home. Write an email to Ayesha giving your views.
In your email you should:
• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about where Ayesha should study.
Base your email on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your email: 'Dear Ayesha,'
Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:
Ideas in the texts and how convincing they are:
Text 1: improve English, international friends, better job – real benefits, last one uncertain.
Text 1: far from family – emotional cost.
Text 1: high fees and costs – serious practical issue.
Text 2: good local universities – fair.
Text 2: saving money by living at home – practical.
Text 2: 'only eighteen' – protective, but many students go abroad at that age.
Text 2: go abroad later for master's – sensible compromise.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Benefits: language, independence, wider experience
• Job advantage not guaranteed
• Cost and possible scholarships
• Homesickness and family support
• Local quality and option to go abroad later
• Own view with friendly encouragement
Short model opening: Dear Ayesha, congratulations on your offer – I've been thinking about your message all day and I want to help you decide.

Text 1: Message from the football club coach
From next month, training will move from 5 p.m. to 6:30 a.m. It's cooler in the morning, the ground is free and players will start school feeling energetic. Text 2: Message in the team's group chat
6:30 is far too early – some of us live forty minutes away and there's no bus at that time. We'll be tired all day in class. Couldn't we just train later in the evening when it's cooler, say 7 p.m., with the floodlights? Write 250 to 350 words.
parts.answer:

Text 1: cooler mornings – sensible in hot weather.
Text 1: ground is free – practical.
Text 1: energetic at school – possible, but early starts could also tire students.
Text 2: forty-minute journey, no early bus – strong practical problem.
Text 2: tired in class – plausible.
Text 2: 7 p.m. with floodlights – cooler too, but electricity costs not mentioned.

Content a strong answer could use:
• Heat and safety in afternoon training
• Ground availability
• Transport problems in the early morning
• Tiredness and school performance
• Evening floodlit option and its cost
• Own view politely expressed

Text 1: Message from the residents' association chair
Last month three bicycles were stolen from the lane behind our houses. Cameras at the corner would deter thieves and help the police find the people responsible. Residents would pay a small monthly charge to cover the cost.

Text 2: Comment from a neighbour
Cameras record everyone who walks past, including children and visitors who have done nothing wrong. Police often do not check the footage. A better idea is a neighbourhood watch with a phone group and better street lighting, which costs less and builds trust among neighbours.

parts.text:
The neighbourhood association is discussing whether to install CCTV cameras in your lane. You decide to write an email to the association secretary giving your views.

• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether CCTV cameras should be installed in the lane.
Base your email on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words.
Begin your email: 'Dear Secretary,'
Write 250 to 350 words.

Content points a strong answer could use:
• Text 1: thefts are a real problem and cameras could deter them and provide evidence
• Text 1: a monthly charge is a fair cost to the residents but the text does not explain how footage would be used
• Text 2: recording innocent people is a fair privacy concern
• Text 2: police may not check footage, so cameras may not help unless they are monitored
• Text 2: neighbourhood watch and lighting are cheaper alternatives that build trust
• Own view e.g. better lighting and a neighbourhood watch first, with a camera trial only if thefts continue

Text 1: Message from your pen friend Wanjiru in Nairobi
There's a stray puppy that sleeps outside our gate every night. I want to adopt it – it's so thin and frightened. A dog would also guard our house. My parents haven't said no yet, but they are not sure. I have always wanted a dog, and I promise I would feed it and walk it every day. It already follows me to school in the morning.

A dog lives for twelve years or more. Wanjiru will go to university in two years – who will look after it then? Vet bills and food cost money, and stray dogs can carry diseases if they are not vaccinated. Perhaps she could feed it and call an animal shelter. Last year our neighbour adopted a puppy, became bored of it within months and left it tied up all day.

• evaluate the ideas and opinions in both texts
• give your own views, with reasons, about whether a children's play corner should be added to the waiting area.

• Text 1: calming children who wait for hours is a clear wellbeing benefit

• Text 2: infection control and daily disinfection are serious practical and safety concerns
• Text 2: faster appointments address the root problem of long waits

Text B: Gardens in the sky
In crowded cities such as Karachi, flat concrete roofs are usually used for nothing more than drying laundry and storing old furniture. A growing number of families, however, are turning them into gardens, and the results are surprising.
The most obvious reward is food. A few large pots and old plastic drums can produce tomatoes, chillies, mint and spinach for much of the year, which saves families money at a time when vegetable prices keep rising. Because the vegetables travel only a few metres from soil to kitchen, they are fresher than anything sold in the market, and families know exactly what has – and has not – been sprayed on them.
Rooftop plants also make homes more comfortable. A layer of soil and leaves shades the concrete, so the rooms underneath stay noticeably cooler in the fierce summer months, and families run their fans and air-conditioners less. Across a whole neighbourhood, green roofs can help reduce the 'heat island' effect that makes cities hotter than the countryside around them.
There are benefits for wildlife too. Butterflies, bees and small birds, which have almost disappeared from many built-up areas, quickly find rooftop flowers. Some gardeners collect rainwater in tanks, which reduces the amount of water rushing into the overloaded drains during monsoon storms.
Finally, many rooftop gardeners talk about how the work makes them feel. Spending half an hour watering and weeding in the cool of the evening, away from the noise of the street, is calming. Children who help learn where food comes from and are more willing to eat vegetables they have grown themselves. Neighbours swap seeds and advice, and friendships form across the low walls between roofs.

3. Produce is fresher

5. Rooms below stay cooler
6. Less electricity used on fans / air-conditioning
7. Helps reduce the extra heat of cities (heat island)
8. Provides a habitat / food for insects and birds
9. Collected rainwater reduces pressure on drains / flooding
10. Gardening is relaxing / reduces stress
11. Children learn where food comes from / eat more vegetables
12. Builds friendships among neighbours

Read Text B, then answer the question.

Text B: Never too late to learn
Many adults believe that learning a new language is something only children can do. It is true that young children pick up the sounds of a language easily, but research and experience show that adults gain a great deal from learning a second or third language – and often learn faster at first, because they know how to study.
The most practical advantage is at work. Employers in tourism, trade, health care and technology value staff who can speak to customers in their own language, and bilingual employees are often considered for promotion or work abroad. Travel becomes richer too: instead of relying on guides and signs, a traveller who speaks even a little of the local language can ask for directions, bargain in markets and make friends.
Learning a language also exercises the brain. Remembering new words and switching between grammar systems improves concentration and memory, and some studies suggest that people who speak more than one language may keep their minds sharper as they grow older. Adult learners often say that studying a new language helps them understand their own language better, as they notice how sentences are built.
There are social and emotional rewards as well. Families separated by migration find that learning a relative's language brings them closer, especially to grandparents and cousins abroad. Reading books or watching films in the original language opens a window on another culture and its way of thinking, which can make people more tolerant. Finally, there is the simple pleasure of achievement: the first time a learner holds a full conversation in a new language is a moment of real pride.

Fifty years ago, the streets of many northern European cities were as jammed with cars as those of any city today. Now, in some of them, more people travel to work by bicycle than by car. How did this change happen?
Part of the answer is that city governments made cycling safe. They built wide cycle lanes separated from traffic by kerbs, so that riders no longer had to compete with lorries and buses. Traffic lights were timed to give cyclists a head start at junctions, and speed limits for cars in residential streets were lowered. Parents who once feared for their children now let them cycle to school.
Cycling also became convenient. Huge bicycle parks were built beside railway stations, allowing people to cycle to the train and continue their journey. Shops, offices and schools were required to provide racks. In winter, cycle paths are cleared of snow before the roads are.
Money played a part too. Petrol prices rose sharply in the 1970s, and parking in the city centre became expensive and difficult, while a bicycle costs almost nothing to run. Many companies give employees an allowance for every kilometre they cycle to work.
Finally, attitudes changed. Cycling came to be seen as healthy and modern rather than old-fashioned. Doctors pointed out that regular cycling strengthens the heart and helps people control their weight. Commuters discovered that they arrived at work more alert, and that in the rush hour a bicycle was often faster than a car. Today, government ministers and business leaders are photographed cycling to work, and children grow up thinking of the bicycle as the normal way to get around.

Text B: Waste not, want not
Around a third of all the food produced in the world is never eaten. Some is lost on farms and during transport, but a surprising amount is thrown away in our own kitchens. The good news is that households can make a big difference with a few simple habits.
The first step happens before shopping. Checking the fridge and cupboards and writing a list helps families buy only what they need. Planning meals for the week makes it less likely that vegetables will be forgotten at the back of the fridge until they rot. Shoppers can also resist special offers such as 'buy two, get one free' unless they are sure they will use the extra item.
Storage matters too. Keeping the fridge at the right temperature, storing bread in a cool dry place and putting older food at the front where it will be seen all help food last longer. Many fruits and cooked dishes can be frozen before they spoil.

Leftovers can become tomorrow's lunch: yesterday's rice can be fried with vegetables, and stale bread can be turned into a sweet dish. Peels and scraps that cannot be eaten can be composted for the garden.
Finally, families should understand date labels. A 'best before' date is about quality, not safety; food is often perfectly good after it. Food that is still good but will not be eaten can be shared with neighbours or given to organisations that pass it on to people in need.

Text B: Around the table
In many homes today, family members eat at different times – one in front of the television, another with a phone, a third grabbing a snack on the way to tuition. Yet researchers and grandparents agree: sitting down together for a meal has benefits that are worth protecting.

Family meals also pass on traditions. Recipes are handed down, children learn table manners and the custom of sharing, and stories about relatives and the past are told across the table. Finally, cooking and eating at home is usually cheaper than buying takeaway food.

Text B: Cooking the sun's gift
In many villages of the Thar desert, women spend hours each day collecting firewood, and the smoke from open fires harms their eyes and lungs. A solar cooker offers a different way. Even so, many communities that have tried solar cookers report that the women feel safer and less tired. Women's groups now share designs and repair the cookers, so the knowledge spreads from one village to the next.

Text B: The river that carries our rubbish
Stand on any bridge over a city stretch of the river after the monsoon and you will see it: a slow carpet of plastic bags, bottles and wrappers. Plastic waste is one of the most visible problems facing our rivers, and its effects go far beyond appearance.
Plastic bags and sheets block drains and narrow channels, so that even moderate rain causes streets to flood. Fish, turtles and river dolphins swallow plastic, mistaking it for food, or become trapped in fishing lines and nets that have been thrown away. As plastic breaks down in sunlight, it forms tiny fragments called microplastics, which are now found in the water used by farmers and, in some places, in drinking water. Fishermen complain that their nets come up full of rubbish rather than fish, and that their catch is smaller every year. Tourists who once came for boat trips now stay away from the dirtiest stretches.
Fortunately, people are fighting back. Several towns have placed floating barriers across canals, which trap rubbish before it reaches the main river so that it can be collected. Volunteer groups organise clean-up days, and the bags they fill are sorted so that some of the plastic can be recycled. Some local governments have banned thin plastic shopping bags and encourage shopkeepers to offer cloth or paper bags instead. Schools run campaigns teaching children not to throw waste into water, and children often persuade their parents to change their habits too. In one village, a small business now pays collectors for every kilogram of plastic they bring in, turning rubbish into a source of income.
None of these steps is enough on its own, but together they show that a cleaner river is possible.

Text B: The true cost of cheap clothes
It has never been cheaper to buy a new shirt. Large fashion chains now release new designs every few weeks, and prices are so low that many shoppers treat clothes as almost disposable, wearing an item a handful of times before throwing it away. But this 'fast fashion' has hidden costs.
The first is environmental. Growing cotton uses enormous quantities of water: a single pair of jeans can require thousands of litres. Dyeing and finishing fabric releases chemicals that, in some producing countries, flow straight into rivers, turning them unnatural colours and poisoning fish. Many cheap clothes are made of polyester, a kind of plastic; every wash releases tiny fibres that drain into the sea. And because garments are so cheap, mountains of them end up in landfill sites or are burned, often within a year of being made.
The second cost is human. To keep prices low, factories pay workers very little, and long hours are common, especially when orders must be rushed. Some factory buildings have been badly maintained, and fires and collapses have killed workers. Workers who complain risk losing their jobs.
Shoppers pay a price too. Cheap clothes are often poorly stitched and lose their shape after a few washes, so they must be replaced quickly, and the money saved is soon spent again. The constant flood of new styles encourages people to buy things they do not need, and many young people feel pressure from social media never to be photographed in the same outfit twice.
Some brands now offer repair services and recycling schemes, and second-hand clothes have become fashionable. Whether these changes will be enough remains to be seen.

Text B: On the mountain
Every summer, climbers from around the world arrive in Gilgit-Baltistan hoping to reach the summit of one of the region's great peaks. Few of them would succeed, or even survive, without the local guides and porters who carry their equipment and lead them through the mountains. It is a proud profession, but a hard one.
The physical demands are enormous. Porters often carry loads of twenty-five kilograms or more for days over glaciers and loose rock, at heights where there is far less oxygen than at sea level. Altitude sickness, which causes headaches, sickness and in serious cases fluid on the lungs or brain, can strike even experienced mountain men. Avalanches, falling rocks and hidden crevasses in the ice make every expedition dangerous.
The equipment problem makes things worse. Foreign climbers arrive with the latest boots, jackets and sleeping bags, but some porters still work in worn-out shoes and borrowed clothes that are not warm enough at night. Frostbite of fingers and toes is not unusual.
There are money worries too. The climbing season lasts only three or four months, so families must live on summer earnings for the whole year. A guide who is injured has little insurance and may be unable to work again. If a season is cancelled because of bad weather, political trouble abroad or, as happened recently, a global illness that stopped travel, income disappears completely.
Despite all this, many guides are proud of their skills and want their profession to be recognised. Some have now trained as instructors and run their own companies, and a few have climbed the highest peaks in the world themselves.

Text B: The sleepless generation
Doctors recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night, yet surveys in many countries suggest that most get far less. Why do so many young people struggle to get the sleep they need?
Part of the explanation is biological. During adolescence the body's internal clock shifts later, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and want to wake later in the morning. Early school start times therefore cut directly into their sleep.
Screens make the problem worse. Phones, tablets and laptops give off a blue-tinted light that tells the brain it is still daytime, delaying the release of the hormone that makes us drowsy. Messages and notifications that arrive late at night keep teenagers alert, and many feel they will miss out if they switch off. Some keep their phones under their pillows and wake up to check them.
Workload is another factor. With school, tuition, homework and, for some, part-time jobs or family responsibilities, the hours left for sleep are squeezed. Stress about exams can make it hard to fall asleep even when a student finally goes to bed.
Daily habits also play a part. Energy drinks, strong tea and coffee consumed in the afternoon and evening can keep the body awake for hours. Long naps after school, though tempting, make it harder to sleep at night. In hot climates, a stuffy bedroom or a power cut that stops the fan can make sleep impossible.
The consequences – poor concentration, low mood and weaker immunity – are serious enough that some schools have experimented with later start times.

Text B: Forests between land and sea
Along parts of the coast near Karachi and in the delta of the Indus, forests grow where few trees could survive: in salty mud that is flooded by the sea twice a day. These are mangroves, and although they may look like tangled, muddy thickets, they are among the most useful ecosystems on Earth.
Mangroves protect the coast. Their dense roots slow down waves and storm surges, reducing damage to villages behind them during cyclones. The roots also trap mud and sand, which stops the shoreline from being washed away and can even help it build up over time.
They are nurseries for sea life. Many kinds of fish, shrimps and crabs lay their eggs among the roots, where the young are sheltered from larger predators. Without mangroves, catches in the open sea would fall, which matters greatly to fishing communities whose income depends on them.
Mangroves help fight climate change too. They store large amounts of carbon, not only in their trunks and leaves but in the deep mud beneath them, which can hold it for centuries if the forest is left undisturbed.
Local people use the forests in many ways. Camels graze on the leaves, honey is collected from bees that feed on mangrove flowers, and fallen wood is gathered for fuel – though cutting too much has damaged some areas in the past. Birdwatchers and tourists come by boat to see flamingos, herons and other migrating birds, bringing income to boatmen and guides.
In recent years, large replanting projects have restored many thousands of hectares along the coast.

Text B: The fading craft of blue pottery
For centuries, the craftsmen of Multan have made blue pottery: plates, vases and tiles decorated with deep cobalt blue and turquoise patterns. Their work decorates shrines and palaces. Yet today the number of workshops is shrinking, and many craftsmen fear their art will not survive another generation.
One problem is competition. Factory-made ceramics, many of them imported, are sold at a fraction of the price of handmade pieces, and most shoppers cannot tell – or do not care about – the difference. Craftsmen also find that the price of raw materials, especially the colours and the fuel for their kilns, has risen steeply, while the prices they can charge have not.
Young people are turning away. A single large vase can take weeks to shape, decorate and fire, and the income is uncertain. Sons of potters often prefer office jobs or work abroad, which offer a steady salary and more respect. Because the skills are passed down within families rather than taught in schools, each young person who leaves takes a whole tradition with him.
Many craftsmen have no direct link with their customers. They sell to middlemen, who resell the pieces in big-city shops at several times the price and keep most of the profit. Few potters have the knowledge or the money to sell online or at international exhibitions.
Some government programmes and designers are trying to help by creating modern designs and connecting craftsmen with buyers abroad, but these efforts reach only a handful of workshops.

Text B: Crossing the Thar
Today, travellers can cross the Thar Desert by road in a day, but for the merchants and explorers who crossed it on camels a century and a half ago, the journey could take weeks and was full of danger.
Water was the greatest worry. Wells were few and far apart, and some had dried up or turned salty since the travellers' guides last visited them. Caravans had to carry heavy water skins, which leaked in the heat. A single mistake in navigation could mean days without water.
Finding the way was itself difficult. Shifting sand dunes changed shape after every storm, burying the tracks and landmarks that guides relied on. Many caravans travelled at night, using the stars, to avoid the heat – but this made it easy to stray off course.
The climate was brutal. Daytime temperatures in summer soared above forty-five degrees, while winter nights could be bitterly cold. Sandstorms could last for hours, forcing travellers to shelter behind their kneeling camels with cloth over their faces, unable to see or breathe properly.
The animals had their own problems. Camels could go many days without drinking, but they needed grazing, and in years of drought there was little to eat. A lame or sick camel had to be left behind with its load.
Finally, travellers sometimes faced bandits who knew the desert well and attacked slow, heavily laden caravans. Many merchants paid local chiefs for protection, adding to the cost of the journey. It is little wonder that those who completed the crossing were treated as heroes when they returned.

Text B: Reefs under pressure
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all marine species. Over recent decades, however, many reefs have suffered serious damage.
The biggest threat is rising sea temperature. Corals live in partnership with tiny algae that give them food and colour. When water becomes too warm for too long, the corals expel these algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but if the heat continues they starve.
The ocean is also becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. This makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeletons, so reefs grow more slowly and become more fragile.
Pollution from land adds to the stress. Fertilisers washed into the sea feed seaweed that smothers corals, and soil from cleared land clouds the water and blocks the sunlight that corals need. Sewage brings diseases.
People damage reefs directly too. In some regions fishermen have used explosives or poison to stun fish, destroying the coral at the same time. Overfishing removes the fish that graze on seaweed and keep it under control. Boats drop anchors on reefs, and careless divers and snorkellers break off fragile branches or take them home as souvenirs. Coastal building projects sometimes dredge or bury whole sections of reef.
Many countries have created marine reserves where fishing and building are restricted, and scientists are growing corals in nurseries to replant damaged areas.

Text B: The emptying sea
Fishermen along the coast have always worked with the tides, taking only what the sea could easily replace. In the past thirty years, however, larger trawlers and finer nets have changed the balance. Trawlers now drag heavy nets across the sea floor, scooping up young fish that have not yet had the chance to breed, along with turtles, dolphins and seabirds caught by accident.
The results are visible in the harbours. Catches that once filled a boat in a single morning now take days to gather, and many small fishermen have sold their boats or moved to the city. Fish prices have risen, so families who once ate fish every week now eat it only on special days.
Scientists warn that the damage goes further. When too many large fish are removed, the balance of the food chain is disturbed. Seaweed beds that shelter young fish have been destroyed by the dragging nets, and without these nurseries the stocks may never recover.
Government rules exist, including closed seasons and minimum mesh sizes, but they are poorly enforced. Some boat owners ignore them, because a single illegal trip can earn more than a month's legal fishing. Experts argue that fishing quotas, supported by patrols and fair compensation for small fishermen, would give the sea a chance to recover.

Text B: The advantage of an early start
Children who begin a second language in primary school tend to speak it with a more natural accent than those who start later. Their brains are still flexible, and they copy sounds and rhythms without the self-consciousness that often makes teenagers hesitant.
Early language learning also strengthens the first language. Children who compare words in two languages begin to notice how grammar works, and many find it easier to understand the structure of their own language. Reading in a second language can introduce new ideas and stories long before they would be met in a textbook.
Critics argue that schools have limited time and that children may master neither language if they are taught too much at once. This worry is reasonable, but well-planned lessons of only twenty minutes a day can achieve good results, especially when songs, games and simple conversations are used rather than endless grammar drills.
Finally, early learners tend to become more open to other cultures. Meeting classmates who speak different languages helps children see that their own way of speaking is only one among many, and this awareness can last throughout their lives.

Text B: Why the bees are disappearing
Farmers have always known that bees are valuable. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar, bees carry pollen that allows fruit trees, sunflowers, mustard and many vegetables to produce seeds and fruit. Without them, harvests of crops such as apples, almonds and melons would fall sharply. Bees also produce honey and wax, which give many rural families extra income.
Yet in many parts of the world, bee numbers are falling, and scientists believe there is no single cause. One of the most serious is the use of certain pesticides. Even when these chemicals do not kill bees outright, they can confuse them so that they cannot find their way back to the hive. Another is the loss of wild flowers. When hedges and field edges are cleared to make room for huge fields of a single crop, bees may have plenty to eat for two weeks a year and almost nothing for the rest.
Diseases and parasites add to the damage. A tiny mite that feeds on bees and spreads viruses has moved across continents, carried in part by the trade in honeybee colonies. Weakened by poor nutrition, bees are less able to resist such infections. Changes in climate also play a part: if flowers bloom earlier than usual after a warm winter, bees may emerge too late to feed on them, and extreme heat and floods can destroy hives.
The good news is that simple actions help. Farmers who leave strips of wild flowers along their fields often see better harvests, and even small town gardens planted with flowering herbs provide food for bees passing through.

Text B: Electric rickshaws: a mixed blessing
The familiar roar of the two-stroke rickshaw is slowly giving way to a quieter hum on the streets of Lahore. Electric rickshaws have been welcomed by many: they produce no exhaust fumes in the street, they are almost silent, and drivers spend far less on electricity than they once did on petrol. Passengers like the smoother ride.
But the new vehicles have brought problems of their own. The biggest is the battery. Many cheaper rickshaws use lead-acid batteries that must be replaced every year or two, and these are often broken up in backyard workshops where lead leaks into the soil and harms the workers' health. Better lithium batteries last longer but are expensive, and many drivers cannot afford them without loans.
Charging is another headache. There are few public charging points, so most drivers charge at home overnight, sometimes through illegal connections that overload local transformers and cause power cuts for whole streets. During the long power cuts of summer, drivers may be unable to charge at all and lose a day's earnings.
The vehicles themselves have limits. A fully loaded electric rickshaw slows down noticeably on bridges and slopes, and its range falls sharply in extreme summer heat, when batteries work less efficiently and wear out faster. Some cheaply made models have weak brakes and frames. And because they are so quiet, pedestrians – especially elderly or visually impaired people – do not always hear them coming.
Finally, the electricity itself is not always clean: much of it is still generated by burning oil and coal, so the pollution has partly moved from the street to the power station.

Text B: Cooling the city
Heatwaves are becoming longer and more frequent in South Asia. In cities, they are made worse by concrete and asphalt, which absorb heat during the day and release it at night, so that temperatures barely fall after sunset. For outdoor workers, the elderly and young children, this can be deadly: heatstroke can cause confusion, collapse and, without treatment, death. Power cuts that stop fans and air-conditioners add to the danger, and water shortages often follow.
Some cities have begun to fight back. One of the simplest measures is an early-warning system: when forecasters predict extreme heat, warnings are sent by text message, radio and mosque loudspeakers, so that people can stay indoors at the hottest time of day and check on elderly neighbours. Hospitals prepare special cooling wards and stock extra fluids.
Cities have also opened 'cooling centres' in schools and community halls, where people without fans can rest in the shade and drink clean water. Charities set up water stalls at bus stops and busy markets.
Longer-term changes aim to make the city itself cooler. Roofs painted white reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it, lowering the temperature inside homes by several degrees. Tree-planting campaigns are creating shade along main roads, and parks are being protected from building. Some employers have changed working hours so that construction workers and street cleaners start earlier and rest during the hottest hours.
Experts warn that heatwaves will keep getting worse, so these measures will need to expand quickly.

Text B: Clearing up space
Since the first satellite was launched in 1957, thousands of objects have been sent into orbit around the Earth. Many are now dead: old satellites, spent rocket stages and fragments from explosions and collisions. Travelling at several kilometres per second, even a piece the size of a marble can smash a working satellite, and every collision creates more debris. Scientists fear a chain reaction in which some orbits become unusable for generations, threatening the satellites we rely on for weather forecasts, navigation and communication.
Engineers are developing several ways to deal with the problem. The cheapest is prevention: international guidelines now ask operators to move satellites out of busy orbits at the end of their lives, either by lowering them so that they burn up in the atmosphere or by pushing them into a distant 'graveyard' orbit. New satellites are being designed to carry extra fuel for this final move.
Tracking also helps. Radar and telescopes on the ground follow tens of thousands of objects, so that satellite operators can be warned and steer away from a possible collision.
Removing debris that is already up there is harder. Experimental spacecraft have tested nets and harpoons to capture old satellites, and others use robotic arms or magnets to grab objects fitted with special docking plates. Once captured, the debris is dragged down to burn up. Researchers are also studying ground-based lasers that could nudge small fragments into lower orbits.
All of these methods are expensive, and no single country can solve the problem alone, which is why many experts argue for binding international rules.

Text B: The home office
When offices closed during the pandemic, millions of people discovered they could do their jobs from home. Many never went back. Working from home has obvious attractions: no exhausting commute, more time with family, the freedom to organise one's day and, for some, the chance to live in a cheaper town far from the office. Yet a few years on, many home workers report that the reality is more complicated. Loneliness is one of the most common complaints. Careers can suffer as well. Several surveys suggest that people who are seldom seen in the office are passed over for promotion, because managers notice those who are physically present. Home workers also pay more for electricity and internet, costs that employers do not always cover.

Text B: Four days or five?
A growing number of schools around the world have experimented with a four-day week, adding time to each remaining day and giving students and staff a long weekend. Passage: Quetta's thirsty future
Quetta, the capital of Balochistan, sits in a dry valley surrounded by mountains. For centuries its people relied on karezes – underground channels that carried water from the foot of the hills – but today the city faces a serious water shortage.
The population has grown many times over in the last fifty years, and every new home needs water. As wells are drilled ever deeper, the cost of pumping rises, and some water has become salty and unsafe. Experts warn that, without action, parts of the city could run out of usable groundwater altogether.

Passage: Why every child should learn to swim
In a country crossed by rivers and canals, and with a long coastline, the ability to swim can save lives. Every year, many children drown in canals, ponds and the sea, often within sight of adults. Learning to swim is one of the best protections – but it brings other benefits too.

At the beach, pay attention to warning flags, as rip currents can pull swimmers out to sea; if caught in one, swim parallel to the shore rather than against it. Do not jump into water without checking its depth. Finally, if someone is in difficulty, do not jump in after them unless trained – throw something that floats and shout for help.

Passage: The hidden danger in old phones
Every year the world throws away tens of millions of tonnes of electronic waste – old phones, computers, televisions and chargers. Much of it ends up in countries where it is taken apart by hand to recover valuable metals.
This work is dangerous. Circuit boards and screens contain lead, mercury and cadmium, which can damage the brain, kidneys and nervous system. In informal recycling yards, workers – sometimes children – burn plastic-coated wires in the open to reach the copper inside, breathing thick toxic smoke. Acids used to extract gold are poured onto the ground when finished, poisoning soil and water used by nearby farms and families. Old batteries can catch fire or explode. Because these workers rarely have gloves or masks, illnesses of the lungs and skin are common, and pollution can affect whole neighbourhoods.
Efforts are under way to reduce the harm. Several countries have passed laws that make manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling their products at the end of their lives. Collection points for old devices have been set up in shops and offices, so that equipment goes to licensed recyclers rather than scrap dealers. Some companies now design phones that are easier to repair and whose batteries can be replaced, so they last longer. Charities train informal recyclers to work more safely and provide protective equipment. And campaigns encourage consumers to keep their devices longer, donate working ones and never throw batteries into household rubbish.

Passage: The invisible plastic
Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres – many so small they can be seen only under a microscope. Scientists have found them almost everywhere they have looked: in the deepest ocean trenches, in Arctic ice, in table salt and in the air of cities.
They come from many sources. Larger plastic items such as bottles and bags break into smaller and smaller pieces as sunlight and waves wear them down. Clothes made from synthetic fabrics shed tiny fibres every time they are washed, and these pass through water treatment plants into rivers. Car tyres wear away on roads, and the dust is washed into drains by rain. Some cosmetics and cleaning products have contained tiny plastic beads, although many countries have now banned them. Paint flaking from buildings and ships adds more.
The effects are still being studied, but there are reasons for concern. Small sea creatures such as plankton and shellfish eat microplastics, which can block their digestive systems and leave them less able to feed and grow. The particles then pass up the food chain to fish and to people who eat seafood. Microplastics can also absorb harmful chemicals from the water and carry them into the animals that swallow them. In soil, they may affect earthworms and the growth of crops. Scientists have detected microplastics in human blood and lungs, but they do not yet know what effect, if any, this has on health.

Passage: How rainbows form
A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through rain while the observer stands with the sun behind them. The sun must be low in the sky, which is why rainbows are most often seen in the early morning or late afternoon. Rain must be falling in front of the observer, and the air must contain many droplets.
Each raindrop acts like a tiny prism. Light enters the drop and slows down, bending as it goes in. It reflects off the back inside surface of the drop, then bends again as it leaves. Because each colour bends by a slightly different amount, white sunlight spreads out into a band of colours.
Red light is bent least, so it appears on the outer edge of the rainbow. Violet light is bent most, so it lies on the inner edge. Sometimes a second, fainter rainbow appears above the first, where the light has reflected twice inside each drop, with the colour order reversed.

Its dense mats block sunlight, so the water below loses oxygen and fish die. Boats become trapped in the mats, and water pumps clog when plants are sucked into their intakes.
The plant also harms farmers. Mats hold back irrigation water and provide shelter for mosquitoes, which can spread disease in nearby villages.
People have tried many methods to control the weed. Workers pull it out by hand and load it onto barges for removal. Some councils use chemical sprays, though these can harm other plants and animals if used carelessly. Biological control, such as introducing insects that feed only on the weed, is another option, but it takes years to test and must be approved carefully before use.

Passage: Guardians of the coast

Passage: When the stars go out
Two hundred years ago, almost everyone on Earth could look up on a clear night and see the Milky Way. Today, a large share of the world's population lives where artificial light hides it completely. Light pollution – excessive or badly directed artificial light – has spread so quietly that few people notice it.
Its causes are easy to see once you look. Street lamps that shine sideways and upwards, rather than only down onto the road, send light into the sky where it is wasted. Advertising boards, shop signs and floodlit buildings are often left on all night when nobody is there to see them. Homes and offices use more outdoor lighting than ever, and modern white LED lamps, though they save energy, are often brighter and contain more blue light than the older orange lamps, which scatters more in the atmosphere. As cities grow, their glow spreads further into the countryside.
The effects reach far beyond astronomy. Many animals depend on darkness. Newly hatched sea turtles find the sea by heading for the brightest horizon, and beach lights lead them inland, where they die. Migrating birds that navigate by the stars become confused by brightly lit towers and may circle until exhausted. Insects swarm around lamps instead of pollinating plants, and many die. People are affected too: light at night disturbs the body's natural clock, and some research links it with poor sleep. Wasted light also means wasted electricity and money – and more greenhouse gases from power stations. Finally, a whole generation of children is growing up without ever seeing a truly dark, star-filled sky.

Passage: Kites, strings and safety
Kite flying has been a much-loved spring tradition in Punjab for generations. Rooftops fill with families, music and food, and the sky turns into a moving pattern of colour. In recent years, however, the festival has also become associated with injuries and deaths, leading authorities to restrict or ban it in several cities.
The worst danger comes from the strings. To cut rivals' kites, some flyers use string coated with crushed glass or metal wire. Stretched across roads, these strings have slit the necks of motorcyclists, sometimes fatally. Metal strings that touch overhead power lines can electrocute the flyer and cause power cuts across whole neighbourhoods. Excited children chasing falling kites run onto busy roads or fall from unprotected rooftops. Celebratory gunfire, though illegal, has also injured people when bullets fall back to earth.
Many people argue that the festival can be made safe rather than banned. Their proposals include strictly enforcing a ban on glass-coated and metal strings, with heavy fines for sellers as well as users, and allowing only cotton thread. Kite flying could be permitted only in designated open areas, such as parks and stadiums, away from roads and power lines. Motorcyclists can fit simple metal wire guards on the front of their bikes, which catch strings before they reach the rider. Parents can be urged to build or check railings on roofs, and police can patrol to stop aerial firing. Supporters say that, with these measures, families could again enjoy the festival without fear.

Passage: Lakes that burst
High in the Karakoram and Hindu Kush, glaciers are melting faster than at any time in recorded history. As they retreat, meltwater collects in hollows behind walls of loose rock and ice left by the glacier, forming glacial lakes. Thousands of such lakes now exist in Pakistan's northern mountains, and some are growing quickly.
These lakes form for several reasons. Rising temperatures make glaciers melt and shrink. As the glacier retreats, it leaves behind a dam of rock and debris, called a moraine, which traps the meltwater. Black carbon – soot from vehicles, factories and burning – settles on the ice, darkening it so that it absorbs more heat and melts faster. Heavy summer rains add even more water.
The danger is that a lake may suddenly burst through its natural dam, sending a wall of water, mud and boulders down the valley. This is known as a glacial lake outburst flood, and it can destroy bridges, roads, homes and fields within minutes.
Communities are preparing in several ways. Automatic weather stations and water-level sensors have been installed near some lakes, sending alarms to villages downstream if the level rises suddenly. Villagers have been trained in emergency drills and know which high ground to run to. Engineers have built protective walls and strengthened bridges, and in some places they have dug channels to drain water slowly from dangerous lakes. Communities are also planting trees on slopes to hold the soil, and local committees store emergency food and equipment.

Passage: The price of a loaf
The price of a loaf of bread has risen sharply in the last two years, and bakers say the causes are beyond their control. Poor harvests have reduced the supply of wheat, so mills must pay more to buy grain. Fuel for ovens has also become more expensive as oil prices have climbed, and the delivery vans need more fuel than before.
Bakers have passed these costs on to shoppers. Some have reduced the size of their loaves, while others raise prices by a few rupees each week. Families who once bought fresh bread every day now buy one loaf for three days, and some have switched to cheaper flour that makes poorer bread.
The effects fall hardest on the poorest households, which spend a large share of their income on food. Children from these homes may eat less at breakfast, and some families have borrowed from shopkeepers to pay for the basics. Local bakeries have also lost customers to supermarkets, which can buy in bulk and offer lower prices.

Passage: Caves in the limestone hills
Beneath the hills of the north lie caves whose walls glitter with crystals. Over thousands of years, water seeping through the rock has dissolved the stone and carved narrow passages, some so tall that a torch cannot reach the roof. Cool air moves slowly through the chambers, and the temperature stays almost the same all year.
The caves are home to bats and to small insects that have adapted to total darkness. Their pale bodies have no need for colour, and some have lost their sight altogether. Fossils of ancient animals are embedded in the walls, offering clues to the history of the region.
These fragile places face several threats. Tourists who touch the walls leave oil from their skin, which slows the growth of the crystals. Miners have cut into some chambers, and the dust from their work has covered the floors. Rainwater running off new roads now carries fuel and litter into the cave entrances.
Protecting the caves requires gates that let bats through but keep people out of the most sensitive areas. Trained guides can explain the rules to visitors, and miners could be offered work outside the caves.

Passage: The quiet bus
The city's first electric buses glide along the main road almost silently, with no clouds of diesel smoke trailing behind them.
