Passage: Enemies of the cotton field
A small caterpillar that bores into cotton bolls can destroy a large share of a farmer's harvest in a single season. The young larvae hatch on the flowers and move into the developing bolls, where they feed on the seeds and fibres. A damaged boll rots, and the cotton inside becomes stained and worthless.
Infestations are worst when the weather is warm and humid, and when the same crop is grown on the same land year after year. Adult moths lay eggs on the plants at night, so the problem can spread quickly across neighbouring fields if nothing is done.
Farmers can reduce the damage in several ways. Planting resistant varieties helps, and ploughing the stalks back into the soil after harvest removes the places where the pest survives the winter. Pheromone traps catch male moths and show when spraying is needed. Crop rotation, with a different crop planted each year, breaks the life cycle.

Text A: The wrong station
[1] Mei had been in Tokyo for only three days when she took the train alone for the first time. Her aunt had written the name of the station on a card in Japanese and English and told her to count six stops.
[2] The carriage was so crowded that Mei could not see the screen showing the station names. She counted carefully, but at the fourth stop a large group pushed out and she was carried through the doors with them. By the time she realised, the train had gone.
[3] She stood on the platform holding the card. Her phone battery was dead, and she could not read the signs. Then she noticed a young station attendant in a blue uniform and white gloves. He looked at the card, smiled, and wrote the platform number and the time of the next train on the back of it.
[4] Twenty minutes later, Mei walked out of the right station. Her aunt was waiting by the ticket gates, holding two cups of hot tea.

Text A: The solar oven
[1] For the school science fair, Daniyal and his friend Rehan decided to build a solar oven. They lined a cardboard box with aluminium foil, painted the inside of a smaller box black and covered the top with a sheet of clear plastic. Rehan's sister lent them a thermometer from her chemistry set.
[2] On the morning of the fair the sky was cloudless, and they set the oven up in the playground with two eggs inside. By ten o'clock the thermometer read sixty degrees. Students crowded round, and a judge wrote something in her notebook.
[3] Then, just before eleven, a wind sprang up. A corner of the plastic sheet came loose, flapped noisily and finally tore away across the playground. The temperature dropped quickly. Daniyal chased the plastic past the canteen while Rehan held down the box with both hands.
[4] When the judge returned, the eggs were still raw. But she asked them how they would improve the design, and Rehan explained that a glass lid held down by clips would stay in place and trap heat better. To their astonishment, they won second prize for 'the best explanation of a failure'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Identify two materials the boys used to build the oven.
parts.answer: Any two of: cardboard box(es), aluminium foil, black paint, clear plastic sheet.
parts.working: 1 mark for any two. The thermometer is equipment, not a building material – do not accept on its own.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What reading did the thermometer show at ten o'clock?
parts.answer: Sixty degrees.
parts.working: 1 mark. Units not required.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Explain what caused the temperature in the oven to drop.
parts.answer: The wind tore the plastic sheet off the top, so heat escaped.
parts.working: 1 mark: wind / plastic came loose and blew away; 1 mark: heat could escape / the oven was no longer covered.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What were Daniyal and Rehan each doing while the plastic blew away?
parts.answer: Daniyal chased the plastic (past the canteen); Rehan held down the box.
parts.working: 1 mark for each boy's action, correctly matched.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Paragraph 4: Give two improvements Rehan suggested.
parts.answer: A glass lid; held down with clips.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'a lid that stays in place / traps more heat' for the second only if clips or securing are mentioned.

Text A: The night the water came
[1] It had rained for four days without stopping when the announcement came from the mosque loudspeaker: the canal bank upstream had broken, and everyone in the village should move to the school on the hill before dark.

[3] As they climbed the muddy path, water was already flowing across the fields behind them. The cart wheel stuck twice, and the second time a neighbour, Ghulam Rasool, put his shoulder to it until it came free.
[4] The school was crowded with families from three villages. Teachers had pushed the desks against the walls, and volunteers from the town were handing out bread and bottled water. Text A: Above the clouds
[1] The group set off from the village of Passu at six in the morning: four students, their geography teacher Mr Baig and a local guide called Wazir, who had walked these paths since he was a boy. The plan was to reach the edge of the glacier by noon and be back before dark.
[2] For the first hour the path was easy, winding between apricot orchards. Then it became a narrow ledge of loose stones above the river. Wazir made them walk in single file, each person placing their feet exactly where the person in front had stepped.
[3] By eleven, Faraz, the tallest of the students, had a pounding headache and felt sick. Wazir sat him down, gave him water with a little salt and sugar, and told him to breathe slowly. 'The mountain is telling you to slow down,' he said. After twenty minutes Faraz felt well enough to continue, but more slowly, with Wazir carrying his rucksack.
[4] They reached the glacier at one o'clock. Its surface was not white, as the students had expected, but grey and streaked with rock, and deep blue cracks ran across it. Mr Baig refused to let anyone step onto it.

parts.answer: Six (four students, Mr Baig and Wazir).
parts.working: 1 mark for six; accept a correct list.

parts.answer: To reach the edge of the glacier by noon; to be back before dark.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Walk in single file; put their feet exactly where the person in front had stepped.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d

parts.answer: Any two of: sat him down; gave him water with salt and sugar; told him to breathe slowly; carried his rucksack.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.answer: It was grey and streaked with rock, not white.
parts.working: 1 mark; must include the contrast or the grey/rocky colour.

Text A: Grandmother's machine
[1] The sewing machine had stood under a cloth in the corner of Grandmother's room for as long as Hiba could remember. It was black, with gold flowers painted along its side, and a heavy iron pedal underneath. Nobody had used it since Grandmother's eyes had grown weak.
[2] During the summer holidays, Hiba decided to make it work again. She found a tin of oil in the storeroom, and her uncle showed her how to clean the dust and old thread out of the moving parts with a small brush. The belt that connected the pedal to the wheel had snapped, so they bought a new one from a shop near the railway station.
[3] The first time Hiba pressed the pedal, the needle jumped and broke. Grandmother, listening from her bed, laughed and told her that she was pushing far too hard. 'Gently, like rocking a cradle,' she said.
[4] By the end of August, Hiba had sewn two cushion covers and a bag for her school books. She gave the first cushion to Grandmother, who ran her fingers along every seam and pronounced them straight.

Text A: When the lights went out
[1] Two nights before her chemistry exam, Amna was halfway through a page of equations when the fan slowed, sighed and stopped, and the room went dark. From the street came the familiar groan of the whole neighbourhood at once.
[2] Her mother lit the emergency lamp, but its battery had not been charged since the last power cut and its light faded within minutes. Her brother suggested using his phone torch, but that, too, was low on charge. In the end Amna carried her books up to the roof, where it was cooler and a full moon lit the page just enough to read her notes, though not the small print of the tables in the back of the book.
[3] At first she was furious. But on the roof, without the light to write, she began instead to test herself aloud, reciting each reaction and explaining it as if she were the teacher. Her younger sister, who could not sleep in the heat, listened and asked questions – 'Why does that one fizz?' – which forced Amna to explain things she had only memorised before.
[4] The power returned at two in the morning. By then Amna realised she knew the reactions better than she had after a week of copying them out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Give two signs, other than darkness, that the power had gone off.
parts.answer: The fan slowed and stopped; the neighbourhood groaned (could be heard from the street).
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Explain why neither the emergency lamp nor the phone torch could solve the problem.
parts.answer: The lamp's battery had not been recharged since the last power cut, so it faded; the phone was low on charge.
parts.working: 1 mark for each, with the reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Give two reasons why Amna went up to the roof.
parts.answer: It was cooler; the full moon gave enough light to read her notes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d

parts.answer: The small print of the tables in the back of the book.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Explain how her sister's questions helped Amna.
parts.answer: They forced her to explain things she had only memorised, so she understood them better.
parts.working: 1 mark: she had to explain / think about reasons; 1 mark: contrast with merely memorising / understood better.

Text A: The audition
[1] The waiting room of the music academy in Vienna had high windows, a polished wooden floor and twelve chairs, eleven of them occupied by young violinists who all seemed calmer than Leila. She had flown from Amman two days earlier, and her violin, which had belonged to her teacher, still felt strange after the dry heat at home; she had retuned it three times that morning.
[2] When her name was called, she walked into a room so large that her footsteps echoed. Three judges sat behind a long table. The one in the middle, a grey-haired woman with reading glasses on a chain, asked her to begin with the scales, then the slow movement she had prepared.
[3] Halfway through the slow movement, her E string slipped out of tune. Leila felt the note go flat. For a second she thought of stopping, as she had been told students sometimes did. Instead she adjusted her finger slightly higher on the string for every note that followed, listening harder than she had ever listened before.
[4] When she finished, the grey-haired woman put down her pen. 'Your string went out of tune,' she said. 'And you corrected it with your ear, not your hand. That is what we are looking for.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Give two details that show Leila had travelled a long way to the audition.
parts.answer: She had flown from Amman (two days earlier); her violin felt strange after the dry heat at home.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept any two relevant details from paragraph 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Why did Leila's violin need retuning so often?
parts.answer: It was affected by the change from the dry heat at home (to a different climate).
parts.working: 1 mark. Must link to the change of climate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: In what order did the judge ask Leila to play?
parts.answer: First scales, then the slow movement she had prepared.
parts.working: 1 mark; order must be correct.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What two choices did Leila have when the string went out of tune, and which did she make?
parts.answer: Stop (as some students did) or carry on; she carried on, adjusting her finger position / listening hard.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying both options; 1 mark for her choice with how she corrected the note.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Paragraph 4: According to the judge, what had Leila done that impressed the judges?
parts.answer: She noticed the string was out of tune and corrected the notes by listening (with her ear), not by retuning (with her hand).
parts.working: 1 mark: corrected the tuning problem while playing; 1 mark: by ear / listening rather than by turning the pegs.

Text A: The mound
[1] The mound rose only a few metres above the flat, dusty land of Cholistan, and to anyone driving past it would have looked like nothing at all. But the team from the university had noticed that, after rain, the ground there was scattered with fragments of red pottery, and that was enough to bring Saima, a second-year student, and five others to spend three weeks digging in the heat.
[2] They worked from dawn until eleven, when the sun became unbearable, and again from four until dusk. Saima's task was the slowest of all: sieving the soil from each layer through a fine mesh and picking out anything that was not stone.
[3] On the twelfth day, among the pebbles in her sieve, she found a small square of baked clay no larger than a postage stamp. One side was smooth; on the other was part of a carved animal – a curved horn and the edge of an eye. Dr Hashmi, the leader of the dig, held it to the light for a long time without speaking. Then he told her to record exactly which layer it had come from before anyone touched it again.
[4] That evening, by the light of a gas lamp, he explained that the position of an object mattered as much as the object itself. Without it, he said, the find could tell them nothing about when the people here had lived.

Text A: Results day
[1] Zara had not slept. At six she was already dressed, checking her phone every few minutes although she knew the results would not be published until ten. She tried to eat breakfast, but the bread seemed to stick in her throat, and she pushed the plate away.
[2] At five to ten she sat on the edge of her bed with the laptop on her knees. Her fingers were trembling so much that she typed her candidate number wrong twice. Downstairs, she could hear her mother pretending to wash dishes that were already clean.
[3] When the page finally loaded, she read it once, then again, then a third time. Then she ran down the stairs two at a time, shouting her mother's name, and threw her arms around her so hard that a plate slipped into the sink and cracked. Neither of them cared.
[4] Later that afternoon, the house filled with relatives who had heard the news. Zara's grandfather, who rarely left his armchair, insisted on walking to the sweet shop himself to buy a box of barfi for the neighbours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraphs 1–2: How did Zara feel before the results were published? Give two details from the text to support your answer.
parts.answer: Feeling: anxious / nervous / tense. Details (any two): she had not slept; checked her phone every few minutes; could not eat / bread stuck in her throat; her fingers were trembling; typed her number wrong twice.
parts.working: 1 mark for an accurate feeling; 1 mark each for two relevant supporting details from the text (short quotations are acceptable). A feeling that is not supported by the text, or a list of contradictory feelings, earns no mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 3: How did Zara feel when she read her results? Give one detail to support your answer.
parts.answer: Feeling: overjoyed / delighted / relieved. Detail (any one): ran down the stairs two at a time; shouted her mother's name; hugged her so hard a plate slipped; 'Neither of them cared'.
parts.working: 1 mark for the feeling; 1 mark for one supporting detail.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: How did Zara's mother feel while Zara waited? Explain how you know.
parts.answer: Nervous / anxious too; she was pretending to wash dishes that were already clean (keeping busy to hide her nerves).
parts.working: 1 mark for the feeling; 1 mark for the evidence with brief explanation.

Text A: The last over
[1] Usman had bowled badly all afternoon. Two of his overs had gone for twelve runs each, and he had heard someone in the crowd laugh when he dropped an easy catch. When the captain tossed him the ball for the final over, with the other team needing eight runs to win, his stomach turned over.
[2] He walked back to his mark slowly, rubbing the ball on his trousers far longer than necessary. He could feel every eye in the ground on him.
[3] His first ball was hit for four. But then something changed. He stopped thinking about the crowd and thought only about the stumps. The next three balls were perfect, and the batsman could only block them. With the fifth, he took the middle stump clean out of the ground.
[4] His teammates mobbed him. Usman stood in the middle of them, laughing, his arms in the air, hardly able to believe what had happened.

parts.answer: Feeling: nervous / afraid / lacking confidence. Details (any two): had bowled badly all afternoon; heard someone laugh at his dropped catch; his stomach turned over; walked back slowly; rubbed the ball far longer than necessary; felt every eye on him.
parts.working: 1 mark for an accurate feeling; 1 mark each for two relevant supporting details from the text (short quotations are acceptable). A feeling that is not supported by the text, or a list of contradictory feelings, earns no mark.

Text A: First snow
[1] Ayesha had been in Toronto for two months, and everything still felt wrong. The bread tasted of nothing, people spoke too fast, and at school no one pronounced her name correctly. In the evenings she lay on her bed scrolling through photographs of her cousins in Hyderabad, and when her grandmother called, she had to end the call quickly so her voice would not give her away.
[2] Then, one Saturday in December, she woke to a strange silence. Outside the window, the street, the cars and the bare trees had all turned white. Flakes were still falling, slowly, like feathers.
[3] She was out of the door before she had finished putting on her boots. The snow squeaked under her feet. She caught flakes on her tongue and laughed out loud at the cold. Her neighbour's children, whom she had never spoken to, threw a snowball that hit her on the shoulder, and without thinking she threw one back. An hour later the four of them had built a snowman with a carrot nose and her own red scarf.

parts.working: 1 mark for each of three details that show the change, explained in own words (e.g. 'she was so eager she didn't stop to dress properly'). Copying without explanation: maximum 1.

[3] Hassan read the note twice. He thought of the night their mother had been ill and how he had slept through it. His face grew hot. He had not even asked why she had taken the bike.
[4] He found Maryam on the roof, watching the kites. He sat down beside her and pushed the envelope into her hand. 'Keep it,' he muttered. 'Uncle Javed can fix the wheel.' She looked at him sideways, and he grinned, and for the first time in days she grinned back.

[1] Every Saturday, Bilal went with his aunt to the cloth market in Faisalabad. He loved watching her bargain. She would pick up a roll of cotton, frown at it as if it had personally insulted her, and ask the price in a voice that suggested she had never heard anything so ridiculous.

[3] In the end she paid almost exactly half of what he had first asked. As they left, the shopkeeper winked at Bilal. 'Your aunt drives a hard bargain,' he said, 'but she is my best customer.'
[4] On the bus home, Bilal asked his aunt why she bothered to argue for so long over a few hundred rupees. She laughed and said that the money was not really the point. 'If I paid his first price,' she explained, 'he would think I didn't respect him enough to bargain.'

Text A: The keeper
[1] For thirty years, Angus MacLeod kept the lighthouse on a rock off the west coast of Scotland. His only company was the wind, the seabirds and, once a fortnight, the supply boat, weather permitting. In winter the waves were so high that spray lashed the lamp room windows sixty metres above the sea.
[2] People in the village thought him a strange, solitary man, and he did nothing to change their opinion. Yet the sailors who passed the rock at night knew him differently.
