[3] When the lighthouse was made automatic and Angus was told he was no longer needed, he packed his few belongings without complaint. But on his first night in the village, they say, he stood at his window until dawn, watching the light turn without him.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'weather permitting'.
parts.answer: Only if the weather was good enough / allowed it.
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'if the weather permitted'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'he did nothing to change their opinion'.
parts.answer: He made no effort to make the villagers think differently about him / show them he was not odd and unfriendly.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) he made no effort; (2) to alter what the villagers thought / their view of him. Words from the phrase itself ('change', 'opinion') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'a promise kept'.
parts.answer: The light was a reliable commitment: the sailors could always depend on it being there to guide them safely.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) reliability / something that could be trusted; (2) it never failed – shone every night as expected. Words from the phrase itself ('promise', 'kept') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The kitten in the drain
[1] The rain had been falling on Lahore since morning, and by the afternoon the streets of Ichhra were ankle-deep. Walking home from tuition, Fatima heard a thin, desperate mewing coming from somewhere below her feet.
[2] Kneeling on the wet pavement, she peered through the iron grating of a drain. A tiny grey kitten was clinging to a ledge just above the rushing water, its fur plastered flat against its body. Every few seconds the water rose and lapped at its paws.
[3] Fatima could not lift the grating alone. She flagged down a rickshaw driver, who grumbled about getting wet but nevertheless crouched beside her and heaved the iron up with a grunt. Fatima reached down, and the kitten, against all her expectations, climbed straight into her hand.
[4] At home, her mother took one look at the dripping bundle and sighed. But by evening it was asleep in a basket by the stove, and her mother was the one warming its milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'its fur plastered flat against its body'.
parts.answer: Its fur was soaked and stuck down close to its skin.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) wet / soaked; (2) stuck tightly / close to the skin. Words from the phrase itself ('plastered', 'flat') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'grumbled about getting wet but nevertheless crouched beside her'.
parts.answer: He complained about the rain, but still / in spite of that bent down to help her.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) he complained / moaned; (2) despite this he still knelt down to help. Words from the phrase itself ('grumbled', 'nevertheless', 'crouched') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'against all her expectations'.
parts.answer: In a way she had not thought would happen at all.
parts.working: 1 mark: completely unexpectedly / she had not thought it would do this.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 4: Using your own words, explain what the final sentence suggests about Fatima's mother.
parts.answer: Although she seemed unwilling at first, she quickly grew fond of the kitten and began to care for it herself.
parts.working: 1 mark: her first reluctance / disapproval (the sigh); 1 mark: she changed and became caring / affectionate towards it.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The stickler
[1] Mr Okafor had a reputation for being a stickler for detail. Nothing escaped his red pen, and he could spot a misplaced comma from across the staffroom.
[2] Yet he was never unkind. When students struggled, he sat beside them until the problem finally made sense, and he rarely raised his voice.
[3] His colleagues sometimes teased him that he would correct the weather forecast if it were written down incorrectly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'a stickler for detail'.
parts.answer: Someone who is very strict about accuracy and notices every small mistake.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for strict about accuracy; 1 mark for noticing small mistakes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'nothing escaped his red pen'.
parts.answer: He noticed and marked every error, even very small ones.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for noticing every mistake; 1 mark for marking or correcting them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'until the problem finally made sense'.
parts.answer: Until the student understood the difficulty clearly.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for the student understanding; 1 mark for the difficulty becoming clear.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The ticket
[1] The ticket inspector moved down the carriage like a shark through shallow water, checking every passenger and ignoring the protests of anyone who had forgotten a pass.
[2] Hamza had been keeping his ticket between his teeth since Lahore, which he thought a very clever way of never losing it.
[3] When the inspector finally reached him, Hamza handed it over with a flourish, and the inspector's face softened into a reluctant smile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'like a shark through shallow water'.
parts.answer: He moved quickly and purposefully through the carriage, searching for people without tickets.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for moving quickly or purposefully; 1 mark for searching for people breaking the rules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'with a flourish'.
parts.answer: He handed it over in a showy, confident way, proud of his cleverness.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for showy or confident; 1 mark for proud or pleased with himself.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'a reluctant smile'.
parts.answer: A smile he did not really want to give, as if he was unwilling to smile.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for unwilling or forced; 1 mark for the smile being given against his feelings.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The biryani
[1] The recipe called for a pinch of saffron, but Nasreen, impatient to finish, simply threw in the whole packet.
[2] The biryani turned an alarming shade of orange, and her husband joked that the rice had been dyed for a festival.
[3] Nonetheless, when the family tasted it, they agreed that the dish had lost none of its generosity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'a pinch of saffron'.
parts.answer: A very small amount of saffron.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a very small amount; 1 mark for a small quantity used in cooking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'an alarming shade of orange'.
parts.answer: A surprisingly strong colour that looked too bright and worrying.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for surprisingly strong or too bright; 1 mark for worrying or unexpected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'had lost none of its generosity'.
parts.answer: The dish was still rich and plentiful, and its flavour was still good despite the extra saffron.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for still rich or plentiful; 1 mark for still tasting good.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Running at altitude
[1] In the highland town of Iten in Kenya, where the air is thin and the red dirt roads wind between farms, running is not so much a sport as a way of life. Before dawn, groups of athletes glide past the houses in silence, their breath visible in the cold.
[2] Joseph had arrived there at seventeen with little more than a pair of borrowed shoes and an unshakeable belief in himself. In his first training run with the senior group, he tried to stay at the front and paid the price: after eight kilometres his legs turned to wood and he was left behind, gasping, as the group disappeared over a hill.
[3] His coach, a former champion with a quiet voice, found him sitting by the roadside. 'The mountain does not reward the impatient,' she said. 'Run with your head first, then your legs.'
[4] Two years later, Joseph crossed the finish line of his first international race in third place. He had spent the final kilometre, he told reporters afterwards, holding back until the moment was right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'not so much a sport as a way of life'.
parts.answer: Running is not just a game or pastime; it is central to how people live every day.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) more than / not merely a leisure activity; (2) it shapes people's whole daily existence / identity. Words from the phrase itself ('sport', 'way of life') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'an unshakeable belief in himself'.
parts.answer: Complete confidence in his own ability that nothing could weaken.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) confidence in his own ability; (2) firm / that could not be weakened by anything. Words from the phrase itself ('unshakeable', 'belief') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'paid the price'.
parts.answer: He suffered the consequences of his mistake (running too fast too early).
parts.working: 1 mark for the idea of suffering a consequence because of his own action.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the coach means by 'Run with your head first, then your legs'.
parts.answer: Plan and think about your pace / tactics before relying on physical strength and effort.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two key ideas explained in own words: (1) think / plan / judge your pace; (2) before relying on strength / physical effort. Words from the phrase itself ('head', 'legs') used in the answer do not earn the mark for that idea.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The mapmaker
[1] The old map was a patchwork of guesses. Rivers wandered where no rivers were, and entire mountain ranges had been drawn from the reports of travellers who had long since forgotten what they had seen.
[2] Yet the cartographer treated every line with reverence, as if each were a promise carved in stone.
[3] When a new survey finally replaced the errors, he sighed and admitted that his life's work had been built on little more than hearsay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'a patchwork of guesses'.
parts.answer: A map made of many uncertain pieces of information that were never properly checked.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for uncertain or unchecked; 1 mark for many mixed pieces put together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'as if each were a promise carved in stone'.
parts.answer: He treated each line as completely certain and permanent, as if it could never be changed.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for certain; 1 mark for permanent or unchangeable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'built on little more than hearsay'.
parts.answer: Based on rumour or what other people had said, not on proven facts.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for rumour or second-hand reports; 1 mark for not proven or not checked.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The garden of silence
[1] Grandmother's garden was never quiet, though people assumed it would be. Crickets chirped in the long grass, and the fountain murmured constantly over its mossy stones.
[2] Yet she called it the garden of silence, because there, she said, the noise of the city dissolved and a person could finally hear their own thoughts.
[3] I did not believe her until one afternoon, when I sat beneath the mulberry tree and found that my restless mind had gone quiet at last.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'the noise of the city dissolved'.
parts.answer: The noise of the city faded away and could no longer be heard.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for fading or disappearing; 1 mark for not being heard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'my restless mind had gone quiet'.
parts.answer: The narrator's anxious, busy thoughts had calmed down.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for calmer or less anxious; 1 mark for thoughts settling down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraphs 1 to 3: Using your own words, explain why the grandmother calls the garden 'the garden of silence' even though it has natural sounds.
parts.answer: Although there are sounds, it is peaceful because the city's noise is shut out and the mind can calm.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for the calm away from city noise; 1 mark for the idea of inner quiet or peace of mind.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The press
[1] The printing workshop in Lahore's Anarkali had once hummed with the rhythm of presses, but now only a lone compositor remained, setting lines of type with the patience of a jeweller.
[2] His colleagues had drifted to the screens of the new digital studios, where a single click could replace a day's work.
[3] Yet the compositor believed that every error he found in the proofs taught him something that no machine could.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'had once hummed with the rhythm of presses'.
parts.answer: The workshop had once been busy and full of regular sounds from the machines.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for busy; 1 mark for regular noise of the machines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Using your own words, explain what the text means by 'with the patience of a jeweller'.
parts.answer: He worked very slowly and carefully, with great precision.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for slow or patient; 1 mark for precise or careful.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Using your own words, explain what the compositor believes. Explain 'something that no machine could'.
parts.answer: Every mistake he corrected taught him a skill or understanding that a machine cannot give, from human judgement and experience.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for learning from mistakes; 1 mark for human judgement or experience that machines cannot have.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The broken vase
[1] Omar heard the crash from the kitchen. When his mother came running, he was sitting on the sofa with a book open on his knees – upside down.
[2] On the floor beside the table lay the pieces of the blue vase that had belonged to his grandmother. A cricket ball was resting under the curtain.
[3] 'What happened?' his mother asked quietly. Omar looked at the ceiling, then at the window, then at the book. 'The cat,' he said at last. His mother glanced at the cat, which was fast asleep in the sunshine on the balcony, on the other side of a firmly shut glass door.
[4] His mother said nothing more. She fetched a broom and a dustpan and handed them to him without a word. Omar swept up every blue fragment, slowly and carefully, and when he had finished, he went to his room and came back with the money from his birthday envelope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest why Omar's book was upside down.
parts.answer: He had grabbed it in a hurry to look innocent / he was only pretending to read.
parts.working: 1 mark for the idea of pretending / a hasty attempt to look innocent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does the cricket ball suggest had really happened to the vase?
parts.answer: Omar had been playing cricket indoors and the ball hit the vase.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Why does Omar look at the ceiling, the window and the book before answering?
parts.answer: He is avoiding his mother's eyes / trying to think of an excuse.
parts.working: 1 mark for either idea.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Explain why his mother is unlikely to believe Omar's answer.
parts.answer: The cat was asleep on the balcony with the door shut, so it could not have reached the vase.
parts.working: 1 mark: cat was outside / asleep; 1 mark: door shut so it could not have got in.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The muddy boots
[1] When Yusuf came in from the rain, his mother was already waiting by the door with a towel, and his father's car keys were missing from the hook.
[2] Yusuf's boots were caked with mud up to the laces, and his trousers were torn at the knee.
[3] "Did you fall off the bridge again?" his mother asked, but she was smiling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest why his father's car keys were missing from the hook.
parts.answer: His father had taken the car out.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible suggestion that the father has gone out in the car.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What can you infer about Yusuf's afternoon? Give one reason.
parts.answer: He had been playing somewhere muddy and possibly had a fall, since his trousers were torn.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible inference about muddy outdoor play or a fall; 1 mark for the reason from the text.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What does the mother's smile suggest about her feelings?
parts.answer: She was not really angry; she was amused or relieved.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible feeling that is not anger.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The storm over the hills
[1] Lightning flickered over the hills, and by the time the first drops hit the tin roof, the vendors had already started packing their stalls.
[2] Mrs Bibi dragged her tray of bangles under the awning and sat with her shawl pulled tight, looking out at the empty road.
[3] "It will be a long night," she told the boy beside her, who had stopped shivering only when she handed him a cup of tea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about the vendors' experience of the weather?
parts.answer: They know storms come quickly and are used to preparing for rain.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for knowing storms come quickly or being used to them; 1 mark for acting quickly to protect the stalls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Suggest why Mrs Bibi is looking at the empty road.
parts.answer: She is waiting for customers, but none are coming in the storm, so she is worried about losing trade.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for hoping for customers; 1 mark for worry about no sales because of the storm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Why was the boy shivering?
parts.answer: He was cold and wet.
parts.working: 1 mark for cold or wet.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Queue at the bank
[1] The queue at the bank stretched out of the door and down the steps. Old men leaned on their walking sticks, and a toddler was asleep on the floor, using a bag as a pillow.
[2] Behind the glass, the cashier glanced at the clock every few minutes, then smiled at the woman at the front as if they were old friends.
[3] When it was finally Tariq's turn, the cashier handed him his money with a wink, and he realised the queue had been moving for a long time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about the bank's service from the queue?
parts.answer: The bank is slow or has too few staff, so customers wait a long time.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for slow service; 1 mark for too few staff or many customers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What might the cashier's glances at the clock suggest about her?
parts.answer: She is tired or looking forward to the end of her shift.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible inference about tiredness or wanting the day to end.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can you infer from the cashier's wink?
parts.answer: She is friendly and playful and wants to make Tariq feel welcome.
parts.working: 1 mark for friendliness or playfulness.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The late supper
[1] Yasmin's brother came home after midnight, tiptoed past the kitchen, and tried to reach the stairs without making a sound.
[2] Their mother, sitting at the table with a cold cup of tea, did not look up. "There is dal on the stove," she said.
[3] He stopped, his shoulders slumping, and muttered an apology that was almost inaudible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about the brother's reason for tiptoeing?
parts.answer: He did not want to be noticed, because he was trying to avoid trouble for coming home late.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for not wanting to be noticed; 1 mark for avoiding trouble for being late.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does the mother's cold cup of tea suggest?
parts.answer: She had been waiting up for him for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark for waiting for a long time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: How does the brother feel? Use evidence from the text.
parts.answer: Guilty or sorry; his shoulders slumped and he muttered an apology.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for guilt or regret; 1 mark for the evidence.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Twelve years later
[1] Rania saw him before he saw her: a tall man at the corner table of the café, turning a cup of coffee round and round without drinking it. Twelve years had passed since they had sat side by side in the back row of Mrs Hussain's English class, sharing answers and secrets.
[2] When she sat down, Tariq stood up so quickly that he knocked the table, and coffee slopped into the saucer. They both laughed, a little too loudly.
[3] For the first few minutes they talked about the weather, the traffic and the price of petrol. Then Rania mentioned Mrs Hussain, and Tariq's face changed. He told her the old teacher had died the previous spring, and that at the funeral he had looked for Rania among the crowd.
[4] Rania was silent. She thought of the letters Mrs Hussain had sent her after she moved abroad, and of how she had always meant to reply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest what Tariq's turning the cup 'round and round without drinking it' shows about his state of mind.
parts.answer: He was nervous / restless about the meeting.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Why do they both laugh 'a little too loudly'?
parts.answer: They feel awkward / embarrassed and are trying to hide their nervousness.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Suggest why they talk about 'the weather, the traffic and the price of petrol' at first.
parts.answer: These are safe, impersonal topics; they are not yet comfortable enough to talk about personal things after so long.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 4: What do you think Rania is feeling at the end, and why? Use evidence from the text.
parts.answer: Guilt / regret: she had received letters from Mrs Hussain but never replied, and now it was too late as the teacher had died.
parts.working: 1 mark for guilt / regret / sadness; 1 mark for the reason (unanswered letters and the teacher's death).

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The interview
[1] The receptionist at Crescent Engineering told Bilqis that Mr Siddiqui was running late, and pointed to a row of chairs. Two other candidates were already waiting. One, a young man in a sharp grey suit, was talking loudly on his phone about the 'easy job' he expected to be offered. The other was reading through a thick folder of notes, her lips moving silently.
[2] While she waited, Bilqis noticed that the water cooler in the corner was leaking onto the carpet. Nobody else seemed to have seen it. She found the receptionist, who thanked her and placed a bucket beneath it.
[3] Forty minutes later, a grey-haired man in shirtsleeves came out of the corridor carrying a mop. He mopped up the water, then turned to the waiting candidates and smiled. 'I'm Siddiqui,' he said. 'Shall we start with you, Miss Bilqis? I'm told you notice things.'
[4] The young man in the grey suit stopped talking on his phone. The woman with the folder closed it slowly. Bilqis stood up, smoothed her sleeve and followed Mr Siddiqui down the corridor, still not quite sure what had just happened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What impression do you get of the young man in the grey suit? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: He is over-confident / arrogant: he talks loudly about the 'easy job' he expects to be offered.
parts.working: 1 mark for the impression; 1 mark for the supporting evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest what the woman with the folder was doing.
parts.answer: Revising / memorising answers for the interview.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Why do you think Mr Siddiqui asks to see Bilqis first? Explain fully.
parts.answer: The receptionist had told him that Bilqis had noticed and reported the leak; he values people who pay attention and take responsibility – perhaps the delay was partly a test.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to her reporting the leak (via the receptionist); 1 mark: he values observant / responsible people, or the waiting was a test.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The thank-you note
[1] Ms Kamran always left the blackboard clean on Fridays, but this week a single word remained in the corner: "Thanks".
[2] The handwriting was careful and round, the kind of writing that belonged to someone who had once been taught by her.
[3] Nobody in the class admitted to writing it, though several of them glanced at Hamid, who was staring fixedly at his shoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest why Ms Kamran would be pleased to find the word "Thanks" on the board.
parts.answer: Someone has shown appreciation for her teaching, which shows that her students value her.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for appreciation or thanks; 1 mark for the idea that she is valued by pupils.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does the handwriting suggest about the writer?
parts.answer: The writer is likely to be a former or current pupil of Ms Kamran who writes neatly and carefully.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a pupil of hers; 1 mark for neat or careful writing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can be inferred about Hamid from the way he stared at his shoes?
parts.answer: He may know who wrote the note, or he feels embarrassed or guilty.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for knowing more than he says; 1 mark for embarrassment or guilt.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The repeat experiment
[1] Dr Osei had repeated the experiment seven times, each time with slightly different chemicals on the bench. Each time, the solution turned the same cloudy grey before settling.
[2] His student, Ruth, kept glancing at the clock above the door, and once she sighed loudly enough for the others to notice.
[3] When the result was finally recorded, Dr Osei simply nodded and wrote one word beside the figures: "Consistent."

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about why Dr Osei repeated the experiment?
parts.answer: He wanted to check that the result was reliable and not a fluke.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for checking reliability; 1 mark for the result being the same each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does Ruth's behaviour suggest about her feelings?
parts.answer: She is bored, impatient or tired of waiting.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for impatience or boredom; 1 mark for evidence from glancing at the clock or sighing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What does Dr Osei's one-word note suggest about the outcome?
parts.answer: The results were repeatable and reliable, and he was satisfied with them.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for reliable or repeatable; 1 mark for satisfaction.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The painting in the corner
[1] The painting hung in the corner of the gallery, almost hidden behind a pillar, though the curator had placed a small brass lamp to light it.
[2] Visitors walked past without stopping, but one elderly woman stood in front of it for nearly half an hour, occasionally lifting a hand to her mouth.
[3] When she finally left, the guard noticed she had left her umbrella behind, though she did not turn back to fetch it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about the curator's view of the painting?
parts.answer: The curator values it and wants it to be seen, though the gallery has placed it in an awkward corner.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for valuing it; 1 mark for the lamp showing care.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Suggest two feelings the woman might have while looking at the painting.
parts.answer: Moved or emotional; nostalgic or touched by memory.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for each of two sensible feelings, with evidence from lifting a hand to her mouth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can you infer about the woman from leaving the umbrella?
parts.answer: She was so absorbed or emotionally moved that she was distracted and did not notice it.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for distraction; 1 mark for emotion or absorption.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The rain at last
[1] The farmers in the valley had not spoken of rain since March. Every evening they gathered at the mosque and looked at the cloudless sky with the same expression of quiet worry.
[2] Samiullah, who had counted the wheat stalks for his grandfather, had started praying for rain before he went to bed.
[3] When the first thunder rolled across the hills, the men simply stood still, faces lifted, and no one said a word until the drops reached the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: What can you infer about the farmers' situation?
parts.answer: There has been a drought or no rain for months, so their crops and harvest are at risk.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for drought or lack of rain; 1 mark for worry about crops or income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Why do you think Samiullah prayed for rain?
parts.answer: He understood how much the village and his family needed rain and cared about the harvest.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for understanding the need for rain; 1 mark for caring about the family's or village's harvest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can be inferred from the men standing still and not speaking?
parts.answer: They were moved, relieved and thankful, and the rain was a long-awaited hope.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for emotion such as relief; 1 mark for the rain being long awaited.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The road
[1] For three weeks the yellow machines had been crawling closer to Bibi Khadija's house at the edge of the village. Every morning she carried her chair out to the doorway and sat with her hands folded in her lap, watching them tear up the old track along which she had walked as a bride, sixty years before.
[2] The young engineer in charge, who was polite and tired, came to explain that the new road would bring buses, a clinic within reach and lorries to carry the farmers' crops to the city. She listened, nodding, and offered him tea, but she did not say a word.
[3] On the day the asphalt was laid outside her gate, her grandson came home from the city on the first bus. He jumped down, ran to her, and she held his face in both her hands for a long time.
[4] That evening she did not carry her chair inside. She left it in the doorway, turned now towards the road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest what Bibi Khadija is thinking as she watches the machines. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: She is thinking sadly about her past / memories (she walked the old track as a bride sixty years ago) and how they are being destroyed.
parts.working: 1 mark: thoughts of loss / memories; 1 mark: evidence (the track she walked as a bride / 'tear up').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does her silence suggest about her attitude to the engineer's explanation?
parts.answer: She is polite but unconvinced / has mixed feelings – she is not ready to agree.
parts.working: 1 mark for the idea of politeness without agreement, or uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Why does she hold her grandson's face 'for a long time'?
parts.answer: She is overjoyed / deeply moved to see him, perhaps because he has not been able to visit often.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paragraph 4: Explain what the last sentence suggests about how her feelings towards the road have changed.
parts.answer: She has come to accept / welcome the road, because it has brought her grandson home – the chair now faces the road rather than watching it in sorrow.
parts.working: 1 mark: acceptance / hope / welcome; 1 mark: linked to the grandson's arrival / the chair now turned towards the road.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The envelope from Peshawar
[1] The envelope arrived on Tuesday, postmarked from Peshawar, but the handwriting on it was unfamiliar to Aliya. She turned it over twice before opening it.
[2] Inside was a single sheet, covered on both sides with questions about the new school, the weather, and whether anyone still kept the old well behind the orchard.
[3] At the bottom, a line had been struck through and rewritten several times, as though the writer had found it hard to say what they meant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest why Aliya turned the envelope over twice.
parts.answer: She was nervous or uncertain about a letter from someone she did not recognise, and may have feared bad news.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for nervousness or uncertainty; 1 mark for the unfamiliar handwriting as the reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraphs 2 and 3: What can you infer about the writer's relationship with Aliya?
parts.answer: The writer is probably a relative or someone from her past who knew her well, since they ask about places from her childhood.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a past connection or family link; 1 mark for a supported detail such as the old well or the orchard.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Suggest what the struck-through line shows about the writer.
parts.answer: The writer found it difficult to express a difficult or emotional message and was hesitant.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for difficulty or uncertainty; 1 mark for an emotional or hesitant message.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The visitor
[1] The stranger arrived at the village just after the monsoon ended, carrying a battered tin trunk and asking for the old schoolmaster by name.
[2] Nobody recognised him, but the schoolmaster's widow took one look at his face and set an extra cup on the table without a word.
[3] That night the two of them spoke in low voices until the lamp had burned out, and the children, listening from the courtyard, heard only the word "forgive" more than once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Suggest why the widow set an extra cup without a word.
parts.answer: She recognised him or realised he was connected to her husband, and she welcomed him kindly.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for recognising him or a link to the schoolmaster; 1 mark for a kind welcome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can be inferred about the stranger's relationship with the schoolmaster?
parts.answer: He was probably someone from the schoolmaster's past, such as a former pupil, and the repeated word 'forgive' suggests an old wrong between them.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a past connection with the schoolmaster; 1 mark for an old wrong or grievance supported by the repeated word 'forgive'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Explain what the repeated word "forgive" suggests about the conversation.
parts.answer: The conversation was about a serious past wrong and an apology or pardon.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a serious past matter; 1 mark for apology or pardon.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The dispatch
[1] The message from headquarters arrived at dusk, and the captain read it twice before folding it into his coat. He called for the drummer boy, then changed his mind and sent him to bed.
[2] Outside, the fires along the ridge had been burning since morning, and the enemy's campfires glowed like scattered embers across the valley.
[3] By morning the captain had ordered the baggage wagons packed in silence, and no one asked where they were going.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Suggest why the captain changed his mind about the drummer boy.
parts.answer: The news was serious, and he wanted to protect the boy from it or keep it secret.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for serious news or danger; 1 mark for protecting the boy or keeping it secret.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: What does 'the enemy's campfires glowed like scattered embers' suggest about the situation?
parts.answer: The enemy was large and spread out, so the army is in danger.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for a large or widespread enemy; 1 mark for the danger to the captain's army.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: What can be inferred from the wagons being packed in silence?
parts.answer: The army is preparing to leave quickly and secretly, so it does not want the enemy to notice.
parts.working: 2 marks: 1 mark for leaving or moving; 1 mark for secrecy or urgency.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Into the desert
[1] The jeep left the last village at noon and headed into the Cholistan desert. Within an hour the track had vanished, and the driver steered by a distant line of dunes. The heat was intense; the metal of the door burned Asad's arm when he rested it on the window.
[2] Late in the afternoon they reached an ancient fort, its walls crumbling but still enormous, rising out of the sand like a ship. A guard emerged from a small gate, wiping his hands, and offered them water from a clay pot.
[3] As the sun sank, the sand turned from gold to deep red, and the air grew cool so swiftly that Asad reached for his jacket.
[4] That night they slept on mats inside the walls of the fort. Asad lay awake for a long time, staring at more stars than he had ever imagined existed, while the guard told stories of the caravans that had once stopped there on their way to distant cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'vanished' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A became rough
B could no longer be seen
C grew wider
D was covered in stones
parts.answer: B could no longer be seen
parts.working: The driver had to steer by distant dunes because the track could not be seen any more. A and D describe a track that still exists; 'vanished' means it had disappeared from view.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'intense' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A extreme
B pleasant
C damp
D changing
parts.answer: A extreme
parts.working: The metal door burned Asad's arm, so the heat was extreme. B contradicts the burning; C and D are not meanings of 'intense'.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'crumbling' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A painted
B falling apart
C newly built
D very tall
parts.answer: B falling apart
parts.working: Crumbling walls are slowly breaking into pieces – the fort is ancient. D is tempting because the walls are 'still enormous', but that describes size, not condition.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'emerged' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A shouted
B came out
C hid
D ran away
parts.answer: B came out
parts.working: The guard came out of a small gate. C is the opposite; A and D do not fit 'from a small gate'.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'swiftly' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A slowly
B gently
C quickly
D strangely
parts.answer: C quickly
parts.working: The air cooled so quickly that Asad needed his jacket at once. A is the opposite; B ('gently') does not explain his sudden need for a jacket.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The lantern
[1] The lantern flickered in the draught, throwing long shadows across the stone walls of the corridor.
[2] Imran moved forward cautiously, his footsteps echoing as if the building were listening.
[3] At the far end, a door stood ajar, and a thin ribbon of light spilled out onto the floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'cautiously' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A quickly
B carelessly
C slowly and carefully
D loudly
parts.answer: C slowly and carefully
parts.working: 'Cautiously' means with care and attention. 'Carelessly' is the opposite; 'quickly' and 'loudly' describe speed and sound, not care.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Drill
[1] When the bell rang, the students at the Quetta school dropped under their desks and covered their heads, just as they had practised every term.
[2] The tremor lasted barely twenty seconds, but the walls shook violently, and a shelf of books crashed to the floor.
[3] Afterwards, the headmistress praised their calm and asked each class to report any injuries in an orderly manner.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'violently' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A gently
B forcefully
C slowly
D quietly
parts.answer: B forcefully
parts.working: 'Violently' means with great force. 'Gently' is the opposite; 'slowly' and 'quietly' describe speed and sound, not force.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The debate
[1] The motion was contentious, and the hall buzzed with murmurs as the first speaker rose, adjusting his tie with exaggerated care.
[2] He spoke with an eloquence that surprised even his opponents, weaving statistics and anecdotes into a case that seemed almost irrefutable.
[3] Yet when the questions came, his answers grew evasive, and the moderator noticed the subtle flicker of unease that passed across his face.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'irrefutable' mean as it is used in paragraph 2? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Impossible to disprove; undeniably true.
parts.working: 1 mark for a meaning of impossible to disprove or undeniably true.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The orchestra
[1] The conductor's baton hovered in the air, and the orchestra, which had been fidgeting moments before, fell into an instant hush.
[2] Then the cellos began a mournful melody, so plaintive that several listeners in the front rows closed their eyes.
[3] The piece was an elegy, written by a composer who had lost his only son in the war.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'plaintive' mean as it is used in paragraph 2? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Sad and mournful, with a sorrowful, pleading sound.
parts.working: 1 mark for sad, mournful or sorrowful.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The bakery at dawn
[1] Long before the call to the dawn prayer, the bakery on Qissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar was ablaze with light. Inside, Gul Khan slapped rounds of dough against the inner wall of the tandoor with a speed that seemed almost careless, though he never burned his hand.
[2] His apprentice, a slight boy of twelve, struggled to keep pace, kneading the dough in a huge tin bowl. Gul Khan rarely praised him, but occasionally, when a batch came out perfectly, he would grunt in a way the boy had learned to interpret as approval.
[3] By sunrise a queue stretched along the street: schoolchildren, labourers and old men who had bought their bread here for half a century. The fragrance of fresh naan drifted across the bazaar, and even the stray dogs sat patiently, waiting for the inevitable scraps.
[4] When the last naan had been sold, Gul Khan wiped his hands on his apron, poured two cups of green tea and handed one to his apprentice without a word. The boy understood that this, too, was a kind of praise.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'ablaze' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A on fire
B brightly lit
C very hot
D crowded
parts.answer: B brightly lit
parts.working: The bakery was 'ablaze with light', so it was brightly lit. A is the literal meaning but the bakery was not burning; C is tempting because of the tandoor, but the phrase is about light.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'slight' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A unimportant
B thin and small
C nervous
D young
parts.answer: B thin and small
parts.working: A 'slight boy' is thin and small in build. A is another meaning of 'slight' (a slight problem) that does not fit a person; D is true of a twelve-year-old but is not what the word means.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'interpret' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A translate
B ignore
C understand
D repeat
parts.answer: C understand
parts.working: The boy had learned to understand the grunt as approval. A is the language sense of 'interpret' and does not fit a grunt; B and D do not fit 'as approval'.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'fragrance' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A taste
B steam
C pleasant smell
D warmth
parts.answer: C pleasant smell
parts.working: The fragrance of fresh naan drifted across the bazaar – a pleasant smell. B could drift, but 'fragrance' refers to smell, not vapour.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'inevitable' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A unexpected
B certain to come
C delicious
D small
parts.answer: B certain to come
parts.working: The dogs waited patiently because scraps were certain to come. A is the opposite; their patience shows they knew the scraps would arrive.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Below the surface
[1] Lina had dived many times off the coast of Aqaba, but she had never seen the reef so vivid. Shoals of tiny orange fish darted between branches of coral, and a turtle drifted past, utterly indifferent to the divers who hovered nearby.
[2] At twenty metres she noticed that her diving partner, Omar, was gesturing urgently. He pointed to his gauge: the needle showed his air was running low far sooner than expected. Lina signalled calmly, and they began their ascent together, rising slowly and stopping as they had been trained.
[3] Back on the boat, Omar admitted that he had neglected to check his tank before the dive. The instructor's reprimand was brief but sharp, and Omar did not argue.
[4] Later, as the boat headed back to the harbour, Omar sat quietly at the stern. Lina handed him a bottle of water and told him that every diver makes a mistake once; the important thing was never to make the same one twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'vivid' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A quiet
B brightly coloured
C damaged
D deep
parts.answer: B brightly coloured
parts.working: The orange fish and coral show that the reef looked brightly coloured. C is the opposite of the description; A and D are not meanings of 'vivid'.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'indifferent' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A unfriendly
B unconcerned
C frightened
D different
parts.answer: B unconcerned
parts.working: The turtle drifted past paying no attention to the divers – it was unconcerned. A suggests hostility, which the turtle did not show; D is a confusion with a similar-looking word.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'ascent' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A agreement
B journey upwards
C dive downwards
D escape
parts.answer: B journey upwards
parts.working: They began rising slowly to the surface. A confuses 'ascent' with 'assent'; C is the opposite (descent).

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'neglected' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A refused
B failed
C remembered
D tried
parts.answer: B failed
parts.working: Omar failed to (did not) check his tank. A suggests he chose not to, which the text does not say; C is the opposite.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'reprimand' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A punishment
B praise
C telling-off
D question
parts.answer: C telling-off
parts.working: The instructor's words were 'brief but sharp' – a telling-off. A is too strong: no penalty is mentioned, only sharp words; B is the opposite.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Market day
[1] The bazaar was thronged long before sunrise, with traders unrolling carpets and hanging cages of pigeons from the eaves of the shops.
[2] Hamid's uncle, a man of few words, haggled with the seller for nearly an hour, his expression never shifting from stern disapproval.
[3] When the price was finally agreed, the seller slapped the rupees into his palm with a theatrical sigh, and Hamid understood the bargain was complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'thronged' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A crowded
B empty
C silent
D decorated
parts.answer: A crowded
parts.working: 'Thronged' means full of people. 'Empty' is the opposite; 'silent' and 'decorated' do not describe a crowd.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Heatwave
[1] By noon the streets of Sukkur lay dormant, the shutters pulled down and the dogs stretched out in the scant shade of the walls.
[2] Ali's grandmother kept her curtains drawn, insisting that the heat was an enemy that could only be outwitted, never confronted.
[3] When the evening breeze finally arrived, the whole neighbourhood seemed to exhale at once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'dormant' mean as it is used in paragraph 1? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Inactive, still or sleeping (no activity at all).
parts.working: 1 mark for a word or phrase that means inactive or still.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Festival lights
[1] The narrow lanes of the old city were festooned with paper lanterns, each one painted in a different shade of red and gold.
[2] Children darted between the stalls, their faces lit by the glow, while their parents lingered by the sweetmeat sellers.
[3] Nobody wanted the night to end, and when the musicians finally packed their drums, a collective groan rose from the crowd.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'festooned' mean as it is used in paragraph 1? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Decorated, or hung with decorations.
parts.working: 1 mark for decorated or hung with decorations.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The ferry
[1] The ferry lurched sideways as the wind caught its hull, and the passengers grabbed the rails, their faces pale.
[2] A young mother clutched her infant tightly, whispering prayers, while an old fisherman remained perfectly still, as if the motion were nothing at all.
[3] Gradually the waves subsided and the ferry steadied, and a ripple of nervous laughter passed through the deck.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'lurched' mean as it is used in paragraph 1? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Swayed or jerked suddenly and unsteadily.
parts.working: 1 mark for swayed, jerked or tilted suddenly.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The final game
[1] The hall was hushed. At the last table of the junior chess championship in Kuala Lumpur, Arif sat opposite the defending champion, a composed girl from Singapore who had not lost a game all week. Her moves were deliberate, each one placed on the board with a small, decisive click.
[2] For two hours the position was balanced. Then, on move forty, Arif saw a chance: if he sacrificed his knight, her king would be exposed. It was a gamble; if he had miscalculated, he would lose. His hand hovered over the piece. He hesitated, checked the line once more, and made the move.
[3] The champion studied the board for a long time. At last she extended her hand across the table – a gesture of resignation – and the spectators, who had been told to remain silent, broke into spontaneous applause.
[4] Arif shook the champion's hand. Only afterwards, when his coach hugged him in the corridor, did he notice that his own hands were shaking.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'composed' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A written
B calm and self-controlled
C proud
D made up of parts
parts.answer: B calm and self-controlled
parts.working: The champion had not lost all week and placed her pieces with decisive clicks – she was calm and in control. A and D are other meanings of 'composed' that do not describe a person; C is not supported by the text.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'deliberate' as it is used in paragraph 1?
A careful and intentional
B quick
C discussed at length
D aggressive
parts.answer: A careful and intentional
parts.working: Each move was placed carefully and on purpose. C is the verb sense ('to deliberate'), which does not fit 'her moves were'; B contradicts the careful placing.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'exposed' as it is used in paragraph 2?
A shown to everyone watching
B open to attack
C trapped in a corner
D removed from the board
parts.answer: B open to attack
parts.working: Sacrificing the knight would leave her king without protection, open to attack. A is a general meaning of 'exposed' that misses the danger; C describes a different situation – a king can be exposed without being cornered.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'resignation' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A leaving her job
B admitting defeat
C sadness
D politeness
parts.answer: B admitting defeat
parts.working: In chess, offering a hand at this point is a sign of conceding the game. A is the workplace meaning; D is tempting because offering a hand is polite, but the gesture here means she accepted defeat.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'spontaneous' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A unplanned
B loud
C polite
D long
parts.answer: A unplanned
parts.working: The spectators had been told to stay silent, so their applause was unplanned and unprompted. B may also be true of applause, but it is not the meaning of 'spontaneous'.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The pilgrims
[1] After the long journey, the pilgrims were weary, yet their faces brightened as the minarets came into view above the dusty plain.
[2] Hafiz, who had walked the entire distance without complaint, now seemed almost reluctant to step forward, as though his legs had grown heavy with doubt.
[3] His companion, however, pressed on with buoyant steps, singing softly to himself.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'buoyant' as it is used in paragraph 3?
A heavy
B cheerful and lively
C exhausted
D hesitant
parts.answer: B cheerful and lively
parts.working: 'Buoyant' means light-hearted and full of energy. 'Heavy' and 'exhausted' suggest tiredness, and 'hesitant' describes Hafiz, not his companion.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The scrap dealer
[1] The scrap dealer's yard was a jumble of rusted bicycles, copper wire and old fridges, each item waiting for its second life.
[2] His regular customers knew to avoid the back corner, where he kept the treasures he refused to sell at any price.
[3] One afternoon a stranger wandered in, lingering over a tarnished silver tray with a curiosity that unsettled the old man.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'tarnished' mean as it is used in paragraph 3? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Dull and discoloured; having lost its shine.
parts.working: 1 mark for dull, discoloured or having lost its shine.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: The old house
[1] The old house had a reputation for being haunted, though Mrs Shah dismissed such talk as nonsense and went about her chores with brisk efficiency.
[2] Only Shazia noticed that her grandmother's hands trembled when she lifted the teapot, and that she never sat near the window after dusk.
[3] "It's just old age," the grandmother said, but her tone was unusually brittle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does 'brisk' mean as it is used in paragraph 1? Give a word or short phrase.
parts.answer: Quick, energetic and businesslike.
parts.working: 1 mark for quick, energetic or businesslike.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Harvest fair
[1] The harvest fair in Okara opened with a parade of tractors, each one decorated with marigolds and streamers that fluttered in the warm breeze.
[2] Farmers displayed their largest onions and most golden wheat, while children sold lemonade from wooden crates and laughed at their own sticky fingers.
[3] By evening the field was a sea of lanterns, and the smell of roasted corn drifted over the crowd.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Identify a single word that describes how the streamers moved in the breeze.
parts.answer: Fluttered
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Paragraph 2: Find a phrase that shows what the farmers displayed.
parts.answer: 'their largest onions and most golden wheat'
parts.working: 1 mark for the complete phrase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paragraph 3: Find the word that tells you the smell moved through the air.
parts.answer: Drifted
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Read Text A, then answer the questions. Paragraph numbers are shown in square brackets.

Text A: Sunrise walk
[1] We set off at dawn, when the sky was still a pale grey and the dew soaked through our shoes.
[2] Ahead, the path wound uphill through pine trees, their needles forming a soft carpet beneath our feet.
[3] At the summit, we stood in silence as the first golden rays spilled over the valley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paragraph 1: Identify the phrase that describes the colour of the sky.
parts.answer: 'pale grey'
parts.working: 1 mark.

Grandmother's kitchen was the warmest room in the house, and not only because of the stove. On winter evenings we gathered there like moths around a lamp, drawn by the smell of onions turning golden in ghee and the comfortable rattle of her bangles as she worked.

She never used a recipe. She measured salt in the hollow of her palm and judged the heat of a pan by holding her hand above it, the way a doctor feels for a fever. When she rolled out rotis, the dough obeyed her completely, spreading into perfect circles under the quick, sure strokes of her rolling pin. She would laugh, take the rolling pin gently from my hand and say, 'Again.' I must have rolled a hundred bad rotis in that kitchen before I made a good one. She ate every single one of the bad ones without complaint, as though each of them were a small gift, and told my mother I was a natural.

The stadium was a bowl of noise. Hassan stood at the end of his run-up, ball in hand, and tried to hear only his own breathing. Six runs needed from the last over, and only one wicket left. The batsman tapped his bat on the crease, a small, confident drumbeat, and settled into his stance. Hassan glanced once at the captain, who nodded, and once at the scoreboard, where the numbers glowed like a challenge. His palms were damp. He wiped the ball on his trousers and took a long breath.

Hassan began to run. The crowd seemed to lean forward as one creature. His feet found their rhythm on the dry grass, and for a moment the world narrowed to a strip of earth, twenty-two yards long, with a single figure waiting at the end of it. He released the ball. It left his hand clean and angry, swung late and crashed into the off stump with a sound like a door slamming on the whole afternoon.

For a heartbeat there was nothing. Then the bowl of noise overflowed.

The letter had been lying on the table for three days. Its envelope was crumpled at one corner, and the stamp had already begun to curl at the edges. Imran walked past it a dozen times before he finally picked it up, turning it over as if the paper might tell him what was inside. The handwriting was his father's, careful and slanted, and it seemed to lean towards him across the page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What effect does the writer suggest by using 'as if the paper might tell him what was inside'?
parts.answer: Any two of: Imran is nervous and reluctant, delaying the moment of reading; the paper is personified as if it holds a secret; it suggests the letter may contain important or frightening news.
parts.working: 1 mark for a clear effect on the reader or the scene; 1 mark for explaining in own words what the chosen word or phrase suggests. Do not credit repetition of the text's words alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What effect does the writer suggest by using 'it seemed to lean towards him across the page'?
parts.answer: Any two of: the handwriting is personified, as if his father is reaching out to him; it suggests a closeness and emotional pull from the letter; it shows how much the writing matters to Imran even before he reads it.
parts.working: 1 mark for a clear effect on the reader or the scene; 1 mark for explaining in own words what the chosen word or phrase suggests. Do not credit repetition of the text's words alone.

practice.stem:
Read the passage below.

Mr Qureshi, the new chemistry teacher, swept into the laboratory five minutes late, his white coat flapping behind him like a cape. Under one arm he carried a stack of papers that threatened to slide to the floor; in his other hand was a glass flask of something bright green that bubbled gently. 'Good morning, scientists!' he announced, grinning. 'Today we are going to make something that glows.' He set the flask down, knocked over a rack of test tubes, caught two of them before they hit the bench and bowed to the astonished class.

For a moment nobody moved. Then someone at the back began to laugh, and soon the whole class was laughing with him. Mr Qureshi did not seem to mind in the least. He pulled down the blinds, switched off the lights and poured a few drops of liquid into the flask. In the darkness, the green mixture began to shine with a soft, eerie light, and thirty students leaned forward in their seats as one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What two impressions does the writer want to convey about Mr Qureshi?
parts.answer: Any two: enthusiastic / energetic (sweeps in, grinning, 'scientists!'); disorganised / clumsy (late, papers slipping, knocks over test tubes); entertaining / theatrical (cape-like coat, bows); quick reactions / skilful (catches test tubes); passionate about his subject / makes science exciting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two different impressions, explained in the candidate's own words. Do not credit two impressions that mean the same thing. Do not credit answers that simply repeat the words of the phrase; the explanation must be in the candidate's own words.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Choose one of your impressions and identify the words from the passage that support it.
parts.answer: e.g. clumsy: 'knocked over a rack of test tubes'; enthusiastic: 'Good morning, scientists!' / 'grinning'; theatrical: 'bowed to the astonished class'.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant quotation matched to an impression from (a).

practice.stem:
Read the passage below.

The old house on Canal Road had been empty for years. Its paint hung in long curls like peeling skin, and the garden had grown wild, with weeds as tall as a child pushing through the broken gate. One upstairs shutter swung loose and banged whenever the wind blew, so that it sounded as though someone was knocking to be let out. Children walking to school crossed to the other side of the road and walked faster, though none of them could have said exactly why.

At night it was worse. The street lamp outside had stopped working long ago, and the house became a dark shape against the sky, blacker than the darkness around it. Sometimes, people said, a faint light could be seen moving behind the upstairs windows, though when anyone looked properly it was gone. Most adults laughed at these stories. Yet even they hurried a little as they passed the broken gate, and nobody ever seemed to want to buy the house, however low the price fell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What two impressions does the writer want to convey about the house?
parts.answer: Any two: neglected / abandoned / decaying (peeling paint, wild garden, broken gate); creepy / sinister / haunted (shutter sounds like someone knocking to be let out); frightening to the children / mysterious (they cross the road without knowing why).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two different impressions, explained in the candidate's own words. Do not credit two impressions that mean the same thing. Do not credit answers that simply repeat the words of the phrase; the explanation must be in the candidate's own words.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think the children 'could not have said exactly why' they walked faster? Give one reason.
parts.answer: Their fear is instinctive / based on atmosphere rather than any real event; the house simply feels threatening.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reasonable explanation.

Stone houses crowded together on narrow terraces, and above them the mountains rose in jagged teeth of grey rock and ice. Even in summer the wind from the glacier carried a sharp, clean chill. Yet everywhere there were signs of care: apricot trees tied neatly to wooden frames, water channels swept free of leaves, and doorsteps scrubbed so white that they shone in the morning sun.

In the late afternoon, women gathered on the flat roofs to dry apricots on wide cloths, turning each fruit by hand. Children carried water up the steep paths in plastic cans almost as big as themselves, laughing and racing one another. An old man sat on a wall mending a basket with slow, careful fingers. Nobody seemed to hurry, yet by evening every task had been done, and smoke rose quietly from every chimney into the darkening blue.

On a corner, a shopkeeper had laid out a cloth on the pavement and was sharing dates and water with the rickshaw drivers who had not made it home in time.

Professor Adeyemi's office looked as if a small storm had passed through it and decided to stay. Journals were stacked in leaning towers on the floor, a dismantled microscope lay in pieces on the windowsill, and a whiteboard was crowded with equations in three colours, some crossed out so fiercely that the pen had torn through to the surface beneath. The professor herself sat in the eye of this storm, perfectly calm, sipping tea from a mug with a chipped handle. She listened to Leila's question without interrupting, then picked up a marker, wiped a small clearing on the board, and began to explain with a patience that made Leila feel, for the first time that term, that her question was not stupid.

parts.label: a

parts.working: 1 mark each for two different impressions, explained in the candidate's own words. Do not credit two impressions that mean the same thing. Do not credit answers that simply repeat the words of the phrase; the explanation must be in the candidate's own words.

parts.working: 1 for knowledge of the image; 1 for linking it to the professor's character.

practice.stem:
Read the text below.

Growing more than vegetables

When Gulshan Girls' School turned a dusty corner of its playground into a vegetable garden three years ago, few teachers expected much. Today the plot produces spinach, tomatoes, coriander and okra, and the harvest is sold to parents every Friday. The money buys seeds and tools for the next season.

Teachers say the garden has become an outdoor classroom. Biology lessons on plant growth now happen beside real seedlings, and mathematics classes measure beds and calculate yields. Students who struggle to sit still indoors often work hardest outside, and several have discovered that they enjoy something they had never tried.

There are difficulties. Watering during the summer holidays depends on a rota of volunteer families, and one year the whole crop dried out when the rota broke down. Some parents worry that time in the garden takes away from preparation for exams, and the plot needs a small budget for fencing to keep out goats from the neighbouring field.

The head teacher, Mrs Rubina Saleem, is clear: 'Children who have grown food understand where it comes from and why it should not be wasted. That lesson lasts longer than any test score.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to the text, give two ways the garden is used in lessons.
parts.answer: Biology lessons on plant growth beside real seedlings; mathematics classes measure beds and calculate yields.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept close paraphrase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Imagine you are a parent of a student at a different school. Your school is deciding whether to start a garden like this. What is your opinion and why? Use information from the text to support your answer.
parts.answer: For: lessons become practical and memorable (biology, maths); students who find classrooms difficult can succeed; it is self-funding through sales; teaches respect for food and less waste. Against: needs reliable watering in holidays (crop failed once); takes time away from exam preparation; costs for fencing and tools; depends on volunteers. A developed answer might support it but suggest a firm holiday rota and limit garden time in exam years.
parts.working: Marking (5 marks): 5 = a clear, consistent viewpoint held throughout, in role, with three or more relevant ideas from the text that are developed and linked to the situation; 3–4 = a clear viewpoint with two ideas from the text, some development; 1–2 = an opinion with limited or undeveloped reference to the text; 0 = no relevant response. Either view can gain full marks. Copying long stretches of the text, or listing points without developing them, keeps the answer below 4.

The bag that lasts for centuries

A thin plastic shopping bag may be used for only a few minutes, but it can remain in the environment for hundreds of years. In many towns, discarded bags block drains, which makes flooding worse in the rainy season. Animals such as cows and goats that graze on rubbish heaps can swallow them, and bags that reach rivers are carried to the sea.

Several cities have banned thin plastic bags. Where bans are enforced, shoppers have switched to cloth or thick reusable bags, and street litter has visibly decreased. Local tailors in one town have even found new business stitching cloth bags from leftover fabric.

However, bans are not always easy. Small shopkeepers say customers complain when they are not given a free bag, and alternatives cost more. Where checking is weak, the thin bags quickly return. Some paper alternatives tear easily in the rain and also use energy and water to make. Campaigners argue that the most important change is in habits: carrying a bag from home every time you shop.

parts.text: Imagine you are a shopkeeper in a market where a ban on thin plastic bags has just been announced. What is your opinion and why? Use information from the text.
parts.answer: For the ban: fewer blocked drains and less flooding near the market; cleaner streets attract shoppers; animals protected; new business opportunities (selling cloth bags); customers will get used to bringing bags. Against: customers complain; alternatives cost the shop money; paper bags tear in rain; unfair if enforcement is weak and other shops keep giving thin bags. A strong answer stays in the shopkeeper's role (profit, customers).

Paws for thought

Animal shelters in many cities depend on volunteers. Teenagers who volunteer walk dogs, clean cages, feed cats and help at adoption days. Shelter managers say that young volunteers bring energy and that animals become calmer and more likely to be adopted when they are handled kindly every day.

Volunteers themselves report benefits. Many say caring for animals reduces stress and gives them a sense of responsibility. Some discover a career interest, such as veterinary science, and the experience looks good on university applications.

There are also challenges. Shelter work can be dirty and tiring, and volunteers sometimes see animals that are sick or have been badly treated, which can be upsetting. There is a small risk of scratches and bites, so training is essential. Some shelters ask volunteers to commit to a regular weekly shift, which can be hard to fit around school and exams. Shelters also point out that volunteers who stop coming suddenly leave staff short-handed.

Two wheels to school

In many cities, the school run means long lines of cars outside gates every morning. Some schools are encouraging students to cycle instead. Cycling is free once you own a bicycle, provides daily exercise and avoids traffic jams. Students who cycle often say they arrive feeling more awake and ready to learn.

Fewer cars outside the school also means cleaner air and safer roads near the gates. A few schools have built covered bicycle stands and run cycling-safety lessons, and some offer a small prize each term to the class with the most cyclists. Parents who no longer have to drive also save fuel and time.

But there are worries. Many roads have no cycle lanes, and heavy traffic, fast motorbikes and buses make cycling dangerous. In very hot weather, students may arrive sweaty and tired. Bicycles can be stolen if there is no secure place to park them, and some parents are concerned about girls' safety on lonely roads. Carrying heavy bags full of books on a bicycle can also be awkward.

Museums from your sofa

Many museums now offer virtual tours. With a computer or phone, anyone can 'walk' through galleries, zoom in on paintings and read information about each object. For students in towns without a museum, or families who cannot afford travel, this opens doors that were once closed.

Same clothes, same chances?

A library on wheels

Every Thursday a converted minibus leaves the district library in Hyderabad and drives to six villages where there is no school library. It carries around 300 books, a small table and a pile of comics that children argue over.

Some parents complain that the van arrives late and that fuel costs are taken from a budget that could buy new books. A few elders believe that children should be reading their school texts instead of storybooks.

Teachers who visit the villages disagree. One says that children who used to read only at school now ask for books by name, and another says that the van has given the girls of one village a reason to ask for more time to study.

Her parents were worried that the year would delay her place at university. Her careers adviser disagreed, saying that employers value people who have managed money and worked with customers.
