Should the school week be four days long?

Several schools in different countries have experimented with a four-day week, adding about an hour to each remaining day so that total teaching time stays almost the same. Supporters point to lower running costs: buildings are closed one day a week, so less is spent on electricity, cleaning and transport. Some schools say teacher absence has dropped, because staff can book appointments on the free day, and that it has become easier to recruit new teachers.

Students in these schools often report feeling less tired at the end of the week and say the extra day allows time for family duties, part-time work or catching up on assignments. However, longer days can be exhausting for younger children, whose concentration fades by mid-afternoon.

Critics also point out that the free day creates problems for working parents, who must find and sometimes pay for childcare. Families who rely on free school meals may struggle when one meal a week disappears. Research so far has produced mixed results on achievement: in some places test scores stayed steady, while in others they fell slightly, particularly in mathematics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Imagine you are a member of a school's parent-teacher committee which is considering a four-day week. What is your opinion and why? Use information from the text to support your answer.
parts.answer: For: saves money on electricity, cleaning, transport; lower teacher absence and easier recruitment; students less tired and have time for family duties, work or assignments; total teaching time nearly unchanged. Against: long days exhaust young children; childcare problems and costs for working parents; loss of free meals for poorer families; mixed or slightly worse results, especially maths. A strong answer weighs these from the committee's viewpoint, e.g. accepting a trial for older year groups only.

Quiet wheels

On the crowded streets of many South Asian cities, electric rickshaws are becoming a common sight. Unlike the familiar two-stroke rickshaws, they produce no exhaust fumes at the roadside and make very little noise. Drivers who have switched say their daily running costs have fallen sharply, because charging a battery costs much less than buying petrol, and there is less engine maintenance.

Passengers often welcome the change. Older people say the rides are smoother, and shopkeepers on busy roads notice that the air feels cleaner on streets where electric vehicles dominate.

Not everyone is convinced. An electric rickshaw costs more to buy, and many drivers cannot afford one without a loan. Batteries need replacing after a few years, and old batteries must be recycled safely or they can leak harmful chemicals. In areas with frequent power cuts, drivers sometimes cannot charge overnight and lose a day's earnings. Some traffic officers also complain that, because they are so quiet, pedestrians do not hear them coming.

City planners argue that the vehicles will only bring their full benefits if charging points are built and the electricity itself comes increasingly from cleaner sources.

Pages or pixels?

E-readers and reading apps have changed the way many people read. A single device can hold thousands of books, which is a blessing for students who would otherwise carry heavy bags. Text size can be enlarged for people with weak eyesight, and many classic books can be downloaded free. Readers in small towns, far from any bookshop, can obtain a new title in seconds.

Paper books need no charging, never crash, and can be lent to a friend or sold second-hand. Some parents worry that children reading on tablets are easily distracted by games and messages.

Cost is debated. A device is expensive to buy, but e-books are often cheaper than printed copies. Printing uses paper, ink and transport, while devices need electricity and contain metals that are difficult to recycle.

Librarians increasingly offer both, arguing that the format matters less than the habit of reading.

Game on

Earning while learning

Counting birds

Every year, thousands of ordinary people take part in bird counts. Volunteers spend an hour noting every bird they see in a garden, park or field, then send their results to researchers. Because so many people take part, scientists can see which species are increasing and which are declining across a whole country, information that a small team of experts could never collect alone.

Taking part also changes volunteers. Many say they notice nature more, and some go on to plant trees or put out water for birds in summer.

There are limits. Beginners can misidentify species, and some areas, such as remote mountains, are hardly covered while cities are counted many times. Some volunteers count only once and never return, so trends in their area are harder to follow. Researchers check unusual records carefully and use statistical methods to correct for these problems, but some scientists remain cautious about relying too heavily on volunteer data.

Learning to play

Learning a musical instrument, whether the piano, the guitar, the tabla or the violin, is often praised for its benefits. Regular practice develops discipline and patience, and studies suggest that musical training can improve memory and concentration. Playing in a group teaches cooperation and listening, and performing builds confidence.

For many young people, music is also a way to relax and express feelings that are hard to put into words. Some go on to teach music, play at family celebrations or earn money from performances.

However, lessons and instruments can be expensive, and progress is often slow, which can be discouraging. Daily practice takes time that might otherwise go on homework or sport, and neighbours do not always appreciate the noise. Some students give up after a year, and parents may feel that money has been wasted. Teachers suggest that borrowing or renting an instrument for the first few months is a sensible way to test a child's commitment before buying one.

Power from the roof

A growing number of households are fitting solar panels on their roofs. For families tired of rising electricity bills and long power cuts, the attraction is obvious: on sunny days the panels can provide most of the power for lights, fans and a refrigerator, and some systems allow spare electricity to be sold back to the grid.

The initial cost, however, is high. A system large enough for a typical home, with batteries to store power for the evening, can cost as much as several months' salary for many families. Batteries lose capacity over time and are expensive to replace. Panels must be cleaned regularly, especially in dusty areas, or their output falls noticeably.

Electricity companies have raised concerns. If many wealthier households produce their own power, the companies receive less money to maintain the network, and costs may rise for families who cannot afford panels. Some engineers also warn that poorly installed systems can be a fire risk.

Despite this, supporters argue that every unit of electricity generated on a roof is one less that needs to be produced by burning fuel, and that prices of panels have fallen considerably over the past decade.

Bringing back the birds

For many years the Saltpan Road district of one coastal city was known for little except traffic and dust. Then a local group began planting small, dense patches of native trees on empty plots, sometimes no bigger than a tennis court. Residents report that the patches are noticeably cooler on summer afternoons, and birdwatchers have recorded species that had not been seen in the area for years. Schools use the patches for nature walks.

Land is valuable, and some residents would prefer the plots to be used for car parking or sports grounds.

The group responds that a small forest is better than none, and that the choice of native species means less water is needed once the trees are established.

Drinking the sea

In coastal towns where rivers run low and groundwater is salty, desalination plants that turn seawater into drinking water can seem like a miracle. Most modern plants push seawater through fine membranes at high pressure, which removes salt and many impurities. A plant can provide a reliable supply all year, regardless of rainfall.

The process, however, uses a great deal of energy, so water from desalination usually costs more than water from rivers or wells. If the energy comes from burning fossil fuels, the plant adds to greenhouse gas emissions. The leftover brine, which is much saltier than seawater, must be returned to the sea carefully; poured out in one spot, it can harm fish and the seabed.

Engineers argue that these problems can be reduced. Plants can be powered by solar or wind energy, and brine can be spread out through long pipes so that it mixes quickly. Some experts say that towns should first fix leaking pipes and reduce waste, which is far cheaper than building a new plant.

For: reliable year-round drinking water for your family regardless of rainfall; harm can be reduced with long outfall pipes and solar or wind power. A challenge-level answer stays in the fisherman's role and may accept the plant only with brine safeguards.

Staying safe in the heat

Heatwaves are becoming more frequent in many parts of South Asia, and temperatures above 45 °C are no longer rare. The body cools itself by sweating, but in extreme heat this may not be enough. Elderly people and young children are most at risk, along with people who work outdoors.

During a heatwave, drink water regularly even if you do not feel thirsty, and avoid sugary fizzy drinks. Try to stay indoors between midday and late afternoon, when the sun is strongest. If you must go out, wear loose, light-coloured cotton clothes and cover your head. Never leave a child or an animal in a parked car, even for a few minutes. Check on elderly neighbours who live alone.

Signs of heatstroke include confusion, a very high temperature and hot, dry skin. Many hospitals set up special heat-relief centres in summer. Weather services now issue heat warnings several days in advance.

Your first week at a new school

Starting at a new school can feel overwhelming. Corridors are unfamiliar, timetables are confusing and everyone else seems to know each other already. Most students say the worst feelings fade within a fortnight.

Before your first day, pack your bag the night before so that the morning is not a rush. When you arrive, look for a map or ask a teacher to show you the main rooms. Introduce yourself to the person sitting next to you; they may be just as nervous. It is a good idea to join at least one club in the first month, as this is one of the easiest ways to make friends with similar interests. Write down your homework in a diary rather than trusting your memory.

Many schools have a counsellor or a 'buddy' scheme for new students. Teachers expect new students to make mistakes, such as going to the wrong room, and are usually understanding.

Buying a used phone

Check the battery health in the settings before you pay, and ask the seller how long they have owned the phone. A battery that drains within a few hours is a warning sign.

Insist on checking that the phone is not linked to another account. Ask the seller to log out and remove any account before you hand over the money.

Pay only in person and by a method you can trace. Walk away if the seller pressures you to decide quickly, since honest sellers rarely mind if you take a day to think.

Making your allowance last

For many students, a monthly allowance seems generous on the first day and disappears long before the month ends. Financial advisers say that the habits formed as a teenager often last into adult life.

A simple first step is to write down everything you spend for two weeks; most people are surprised by how much goes on snacks and phone top-ups. Once you know where the money goes, decide on a fixed amount to save at the start of each month, rather than saving whatever is left over at the end. Before buying something expensive, wait at least a week: if you still want it, it is probably a sensible purchase. Avoid lending money you cannot afford to lose.

Banks in some countries offer accounts designed for young people, and a few schools now teach basic money management. Surveys suggest that teenagers who save regularly are less likely to borrow money as young adults.

Trekking in the high valleys

Each summer, hikers head for the northern mountains, drawn by glaciers, lakes and some of the highest peaks on Earth. The scenery is spectacular, but the conditions can change quickly, and every year some trekkers have to be rescued.

Altitude is the first danger. Above about 2,500 metres, the air contains less oxygen, and climbing too fast can cause headaches, nausea and, in serious cases, life-threatening illness. Experienced guides recommend that you climb slowly, spending an extra night at a middle altitude to let your body adjust. If symptoms become worse, go down immediately rather than waiting to see if they improve.

Weather is the second danger. Always tell someone your route and when you expect to return. Carry warm layers even on a sunny morning, because temperatures can drop sharply in the afternoon. Hiring a local guide or porter not only improves safety but also supports the mountain economy.

Litter is a growing problem on popular routes, and some local groups now organise clean-up treks.

parts.answer: Any three: climb slowly / spend an extra night at a middle altitude; go down immediately if symptoms get worse; tell someone your route and return time; carry warm layers even on a sunny morning; hire a local guide or porter.

A cat in the family

Cats are popular pets because they are independent and do not need to be walked. However, they still need care and attention, and an unhappy cat may scratch furniture or stop using its litter tray.

Vets advise that a new cat should be given a quiet room for its first few days, with food, water and a litter tray, so that it can get used to new smells and sounds. Take your cat for vaccinations and a health check soon after it arrives. Feed it food made for cats rather than leftovers from the family meal, as some human foods, such as onions, are harmful to them. Provide a scratching post to protect your furniture.

Cats often sleep for more than twelve hours a day, so a sleepy cat is not necessarily ill. Many live for fifteen years or more, so adopting one is a long-term commitment for the whole family.

A garden on the balcony

You do not need a large garden to grow your own food. A sunny balcony or rooftop can produce tomatoes, chillies, mint and spinach.

Choose containers with holes in the bottom so that water can drain away; roots sitting in water soon rot. Use a mixture of soil and compost rather than plain soil from the street, which may be poor or contain litter. Most vegetables need at least five or six hours of sunlight, so place pots where the sun reaches them for most of the day. In hot weather, water early in the morning or in the evening, when less water is lost to evaporation. Start with easy plants such as mint or spinach before trying more demanding crops.

Growing even a few herbs can save money and encourages children to try new vegetables. Some families say tending the plants has become a relaxing evening routine.

Use a float board to kick your legs, and keep your head low. Practise for a short time each day rather than one long session once a week.

Swim only where a lifeguard is present, and never swim alone, even if you are a confident swimmer. The most dangerous moment is often when a beginner begins to feel panic.

After an argument

When a disagreement with a friend becomes heated, take a short walk before you say anything else. Your voice will be calmer when you return, and you will be less likely to say something you regret.

Listen to what the other person says without interrupting, even if you disagree. Repeat their main point in your own words so that they know you have understood.

Most friendships survive small quarrels. Apologising for your part in the argument, even a small part, is often the quickest way to repair the friendship.

Revision that works

Many students spend hours reading their notes again and again and highlighting almost every line, yet feel unprepared on exam day. Psychologists who study memory have found that some popular habits are much less effective than they feel.

Re-reading gives a false sense of confidence because familiar text feels easy. Testing yourself is far more powerful: close the book and write down everything you can remember, then check what you missed. Spread your revision over several weeks; short sessions on many days beat one long session the night before. Mix different topics in a single session rather than doing all of one topic at once, as this trains you to choose the right method in the exam. Past-style questions should be answered under timed conditions at least a few times.

Sleep also matters. During sleep, the brain strengthens memories formed during the day, so staying up all night before an exam can do more harm than good.

parts.answer: Any three: test yourself (close the book, write what you remember, then check); spread revision over several weeks / short sessions on many days; mix different topics in one session; answer questions under timed conditions. (Accept: do not stay up all night before an exam / get enough sleep, as it is clearly implied advice.)

Getting around a new city abroad

Arriving in a foreign city for the first time can be exciting and bewildering. Ticket machines are in an unfamiliar language, maps show routes in a tangle of colours, and announcements are too fast to follow.

Before you travel, download an offline map of the city, so that you are not relying on mobile data, which may be expensive. Many cities sell a travel card that can be topped up and used on buses, trams and the metro; it is usually cheaper than buying single tickets. When you arrive, keep a written note of your hotel address in the local language to show a taxi driver if your phone runs out of charge. On crowded trains, carry your bag in front of you.

Public transport in many large cities runs until after midnight, though services are less frequent at night. Most metro systems also have staff at ticket offices who can help visitors.

Your first interview

Whether you are applying for a volunteer post, a place at college or a part-time job, an interview can be nerve-racking. Interviewers know that young applicants have limited experience, and they are often more interested in attitude than in a long list of achievements.

Research the organisation beforehand so that you can explain why you want to join it. Prepare two or three examples from school or community life that show qualities such as reliability or teamwork. On the day, arrive ten minutes early, and switch your phone to silent before you go in. Listen to each question fully before answering, and if you do not understand it, ask politely for it to be repeated. At the end, have a question of your own ready; it shows genuine interest.

Many interviewers make up their minds within the first few minutes, so first impressions matter. A failed interview is still useful practice for the next one.

Empty any container that holds standing water, including flower pots, old tyres and buckets, at least once a week. Dengue mosquitoes breed in clean water, so even a small bottle cap can be a home for their eggs.
